title: Giving Measurements a Place
topic: From a measurement to a calculation
blurb: Three thermometers give us three readings. Before we can calculate with them, we need to decide how those readings are stored, which position belongs to which thermometer, and what an operation should do to the collection.
openingTitle: How Do We Give the Computer Our Measurements?
opening: Suppose Botie checks three greenhouses each morning. Today the thermometers read 12, 18, and 24 degrees Celsius. We can write those readings on paper, but a program needs them in a form it can work with.

Let's start with one reading, then work out how to keep all three together. Python gives us several ways to organise information. We will see why a list is useful for keeping entries in order, a dictionary is useful for finding a named reading, and a NumPy array is useful for calculating with the readings.

history.title: When One Calculation Needed to Work on Many Measurements

sources.title: Harris and colleagues: Array programming with NumPy (2020)
Python: lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries

blocks: Scientific programs often repeat the same operation on long collections of measurements. Writing a separate instruction for every reading makes the program harder to inspect, while writing a Python loop for every numerical operation can add overhead.

The NumPy authors' 2020 account describes an array model that combines compact expressions with compiled numerical operations. The useful idea for us is simple: organise the readings once, then express a calculation for the collection. Our greenhouse readings are invented, not measurements from that paper.

intuition.title: Give every greenhouse a position
intuition.explanation: Keep the same greenhouse order throughout the calculation. A result in the first position still belongs to the first greenhouse.

intuition.title: Apply the conversion to each reading
intuition.explanation: The conversion needs a scale and an offset. Neither depends on which greenhouse supplied the reading.

intuition.title: Read the answers in the original order
intuition.explanation: We now have the same observations in Fahrenheit. Changing the units has not changed the temperature in any greenhouse.

parts.title: 1. A Value, a Name, and a Collection
paragraphs: Suppose we only had one thermometer. We could keep its reading under one name and use that name whenever we needed the temperature. Now suppose Botie has a hundred thermometers. Giving every reading its own variable would make even a simple calculation tedious. We need a way to keep related readings together.

A data structure is a way of organising information so that we can find it and work with it. Python gives us several choices. We will start with a list, which keeps items in a sequence. The position of an item is called its index.
parts.calculation:
Position:      0    1    2
Greenhouse: North Middle South
Celsius:      12   18   24
interpretation: Positions start at zero. Position zero identifies the first reading; it does not mean that the temperature is zero. We have decided that the first position belongs to the north greenhouse.

examples.title: Start with one reading, then keep three together
paragraphs: The equals sign assigns a value to a name. Here, north refers to one number, which we call a scalar. Square brackets with comma-separated items create a list. Putting square brackets after the list's name retrieves an item instead.
The print function displays what we give it. The len function tells us how many items the list contains. Parentheses hold the information passed to a function.
examples.code:
north = 12
readings = [north, 18, 24]

print(north)
print(readings)
print(readings[0])
print(len(readings))
interpretation: The first line is one number. The second is our collection. The third retrieves the north greenhouse's reading, and the fourth counts the entries. A list can contain other kinds of values too, but this one contains only temperatures.

examples.title: Correct one entry without replacing the whole report
paragraphs: Suppose the middle thermometer was misread, and Botie also checks a fourth greenhouse. A list is mutable: we can change its contents after creating it. Assigning to an index replaces that item. Calling append adds an item at the end. An operation attached to an object with a dot, such as append, is called a method.
A slice retrieves a range of positions. The starting position is included and the stopping position is excluded. This example asks for positions one and two.
examples.code:
readings = [12, 18, 24]
readings[1] = 19
readings.append(21)

print(readings)
print(readings[1:3])
interpretation: The corrected reading stays in the middle greenhouse's position. The fourth greenhouse goes at the end. Taking the slice does not remove entries from the original list. Each worked example on these pages starts with its own data, so this correction does not carry into the next example.

parts.title: 2. Apply the Rule One Reading at a Time
paragraphs: Before asking Python to calculate for a whole collection, let's work through one reading. Celsius and Fahrenheit use different sized degrees and different zero points. We first multiply by the scale between their degree sizes. Then we add the offset between their zero points.
interpretation: These are three separate conversions. We are changing the units of each observation, so we still need one answer per greenhouse.

examples.title: Give each step a name
paragraphs: In Python, the asterisk means multiplication. We can store the intermediate result under a name, then use it in the next instruction. This lets us inspect each step before applying the rule to all three readings.
examples.code:
celsius = 12
scaled = celsius * 1.8
fahrenheit = scaled + 32

print(scaled)
print(fahrenheit)
interpretation: The scaled value is only an intermediate result. We must also shift the zero point before reporting Fahrenheit. Both variables here refer to single numbers, not lists.

parts.title: 3. Tell the Computer Which Kind of Number We Need
paragraphs: Our list keeps the readings together, but Python does not interpret every list operation as arithmetic on its entries. We need a numerical collection whose operations have that meaning. NumPy supplies one: the array, whose Python type is called ndarray.

For the ordinary numerical arrays in these lessons, every entry uses the same data type, or dtype. Integers store whole numbers. Floating-point numbers allow fractional readings, although many decimals are represented approximately. The data type describes how values are stored; it does not record their units.
interpretation: We will explicitly request floating-point storage because temperatures and their conversions may contain fractions.

examples.title: Turn the list into a numerical array
paragraphs: Importing NumPy makes its tools available. The name np is a short name we choose for it. The array function takes our Python list and creates an array. The named argument dtype tells it which kind of values to store.
The dtype attribute reports that choice. The tolist method returns an ordinary Python list, which gives us a convenient way to print the entries. It does not change the array into a list in place.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = [12, 18, 24]
celsius = np.array(readings, dtype=float)

print(celsius.tolist())
print(celsius.dtype)
interpretation: The decimal points show the floating-point values in the returned list. The reported float64 is NumPy's 64-bit floating-point type used here. The three positions still belong to the same three greenhouses.

examples.title: The same multiplication sign can do two different things
paragraphs: Let's multiply a list and an array by the same whole number. Before reading the output, consider what each collection is designed to do: the list supports repeating a sequence; the numerical array supports multiplying its entries.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = [12, 18, 24]
celsius = np.array(readings)

print(readings * 2)
print((celsius * 2).tolist())
interpretation: Repeating the list gives six entries. Multiplying the array gives three doubled values. If we want to calculate a new temperature for each greenhouse, we need the second behaviour.

examples.title: Convert the collection and prepare it for display
paragraphs: Now we can apply the two conversion steps to the array. NumPy performs the arithmetic for each entry. NumPy's round function takes the result and a number of decimal places. We keep that rounded result separately, then turn it into a list for printing.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

celsius = np.array([12, 18, 24], dtype=float)
scaled = celsius * 1.8
fahrenheit = scaled + 32
displayed = np.round(fahrenheit, 1)

print(displayed.tolist())
print(celsius.tolist())
interpretation: We have one converted value per greenhouse. These arithmetic expressions produce new arrays, so the original Celsius readings are still available. Rounding is a display choice; it does not make floating-point arithmetic exact.

parts.title: 4. Check the Meaning as Well as the Numbers
paragraphs: A plausible number is not enough. We need the right units, the right order, and the right number of results. A familiar reference temperature helps us check the conversion.
parts.calculation:
Freezing point: (0 × 1.8) + 32 = 32
Boiling point at standard atmospheric pressure: (100 × 1.8) + 32 = 212
interpretation: There is another question our array cannot answer on its own: which entry belongs to which greenhouse? We must keep that information with the report.

examples.title: Use a dictionary when the name is how we find the reading
paragraphs: A dictionary associates a key with a value. Here each key is a greenhouse name, written as a quoted string of text. Its value is the temperature. Curly braces contain the entries, and a colon separates each key from its value.
A list lookup uses a position. This dictionary lookup uses a name. When we later need a numerical array, we can first request the readings in an explicit order.
examples.code:
by_greenhouse = {
    "north": 12,
    "middle": 18,
    "south": 24,
}

print(by_greenhouse["north"])
ordered_readings = [
    by_greenhouse["north"],
    by_greenhouse["middle"],
    by_greenhouse["south"],
]
print(ordered_readings)
interpretation: The dictionary is useful for looking up a named reading; the array is useful for numerical calculations across readings. Neither structure knows that these numbers are Celsius. That meaning still belongs in our variable names, labels, and explanation.

title: Which Direction Are We Adding?
topic: From a measurement to a calculation
blurb: A table can hold several greenhouses across several days. Adding across a row answers a different question from adding down a column. We need to keep that distinction when we ask an array to calculate.
openingTitle: Which Average Did We Actually Ask For?
opening: Botie now has two days of temperatures for three greenhouses. We could ask for the average temperature of each greenhouse, or the average across all greenhouses on each day. Both are reasonable questions, but they have different answers.
The entries alone cannot tell the computer which question we mean. We need to describe the table's layout and say which direction the calculation should combine.

history.title: Keeping the Meaning of a Scientific Table

sources.title: Python: lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries

blocks: Scientific records commonly separate observations from the things measured about them. Array programming keeps those distinctions as axes, so a calculation can combine one direction while preserving the others.

NumPy's documented reduction operations make the chosen axis explicit. Our two-day greenhouse table is an invented example of why that choice matters. We are using an established array convention, not attributing the invention of tables or averages to NumPy.

intuition.title: Name both directions
intuition.explanation: Rows are days; columns are greenhouses. Keep these labels in view before reducing anything.

intuition.title: Keep the greenhouses separate
intuition.explanation: Combine the two days within each column. We should end with three answers.

intuition.title: Or keep the days separate
intuition.explanation: Combining each row gives a daily summary instead. That leaves two answers.

parts.title: 1. Give Each Axis a Job
paragraphs: One list was enough for one morning. With several mornings, a flat list would make us remember where each day begins and ends. Instead, let's keep one list per day and put those lists inside another list. This is a nested list.
We can use this arrangement to create a two-dimensional NumPy array. Its first axis follows the days and its second follows the greenhouses. An axis is a direction in the organisation of an array.
interpretation: A scalar is one value. A one-dimensional array is a sequence of values. Our two-dimensional array is a table of values, which we can also interpret as a matrix. The number of axes is different from the number of entries.

examples.title: Build the table one row at a time
paragraphs: The outer list contains two items, each of which is itself a list. The first lookup chooses Tuesday's list. The second lookup chooses the middle greenhouse within that list. NumPy accepts these equally long rows as a rectangular numerical array.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

days = [
    [10, 20, 30],
    [14, 22, 36],
]
print(days[1])
print(days[1][1])

temperatures = np.array(days, dtype=float)
print(temperatures.tolist())
interpretation: The double square brackets in the final output preserve the rows: this is a list containing lists. A Python nested list could have unequal row lengths, but those rows would not form the regular numerical table we need here.

examples.title: Read the shape as a tuple of axis lengths
paragraphs: A tuple is an ordered collection whose entries cannot be replaced after it is created. Python commonly writes tuples with parentheses. NumPy reports an array's shape as a tuple: one length for each axis, in axis order.
The ndim attribute counts axes. The size attribute counts all entries. These describe different things, so let's print each one separately.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

temperatures = np.array([
    [10, 20, 30],
    [14, 22, 36],
])
shape = temperatures.shape

print(shape)
print(shape[0])
print(shape[1])
print(temperatures.ndim)
print(temperatures.size)
interpretation: There are two day rows, three greenhouse columns, two axes, and six temperatures. The shape tuple records the lengths; it contains none of the temperatures. We can index that tuple to read a length, but we cannot replace one of its entries as we could with a list.

examples.title: Ask for one reading, one day, or one greenhouse
paragraphs: In a two-dimensional array, the comma inside square brackets separates the row selection from the column selection. A colon by itself means all positions along that axis. So we can choose one row and one column, all columns of a row, or all rows of a column.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

temperatures = np.array([
    [10, 20, 30],
    [14, 22, 36],
])

print(temperatures[1, 1])
print(temperatures[0, :].tolist())
print(temperatures[:, 1].tolist())
interpretation: The first result is Tuesday's middle greenhouse reading. The second is all of Monday. The third follows the middle greenhouse across both days. Selecting one row or one column this way leaves a one-dimensional array.

parts.title: 2. Remove the Direction We Combine
paragraphs: To find one mean per greenhouse, we need to combine the days while keeping the greenhouses separate. The days occupy axis zero, so that is the axis we reduce. A reduction combines several entries into a summary.
interpretation: The day axis disappears because its readings have been combined. The remaining entries belong to the three greenhouses.

examples.title: Keep one answer per greenhouse
paragraphs: The mean method calculates an average. Its axis argument says which direction to combine. The result's shape is a one-entry tuple. The trailing comma is how Python distinguishes a one-entry tuple from parentheses around a single number.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

temperatures = np.array([
    [10, 20, 30],
    [14, 22, 36],
])
per_greenhouse = temperatures.mean(axis=0)

print(per_greenhouse.tolist())
print(per_greenhouse.shape)
interpretation: The result has one axis of length three. It is not a table with three rows and an unspecified number of columns. It has no second axis.

parts.title: 3. Ask the Other Question
paragraphs: For one mean per day, we combine the greenhouse axis instead. Reducing axis one leaves the day axis. The same six temperatures now answer a different question.
interpretation: Neither summary is inherently better. The useful one depends on whether Botie needs a greenhouse comparison or a daily report.

examples.title: Compare a daily summary with a single overall value
paragraphs: Providing axis one gives a result for each day. Leaving out axis asks mean to combine every entry into one scalar. That single number no longer keeps either day or greenhouse separate.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

temperatures = np.array([
    [10, 20, 30],
    [14, 22, 36],
])
per_day = temperatures.mean(axis=1)

print(per_day.tolist())
print(per_day.shape)
print(temperatures.mean())
interpretation: The list has two daily means. The final number averages all six readings. Before writing a reduction, say what one answer should represent and how many answers you need.

parts.title: 4. Predict the Shape Before Running the Code
paragraphs: We now have a way to check whether an operation left us the right kind of result: inspect its shape. That check is useful before reading any particular number. The right shape does not prove the numbers are correct, but the wrong shape can reveal that we answered a different question.

There is one more detail to understand before editing a selected row. A NumPy slice can be a view, meaning it refers to part of the original array's storage. Giving that view a new variable name does not give it independent data.
interpretation: If Botie wants to try a correction without altering the saved readings, we need a copy.

examples.title: A view shares readings; a copy keeps its own
paragraphs: We select Monday's row twice. One selection remains a view. For the other, we call copy to give it its own numerical storage. Then we change the first entry of each selection.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

temperatures = np.array([
    [10, 20, 30],
    [14, 22, 36],
])
monday_view = temperatures[0, :]
monday_copy = temperatures[0, :].copy()

monday_view[0] = 11
monday_copy[0] = 99

print(temperatures[0, :].tolist())
print(monday_copy.tolist())
interpretation: Changing the view changed Monday in the original table. Changing the copy did not. The workshop will summarise the readings, and the challenges will calculate both kinds of mean without modifying their inputs.

title: Preparing the Arrays We Need
topic: From a measurement to a calculation
blurb: Botie needs a place for tomorrow's readings and a set of times at which to collect them. We can describe those arrangements directly instead of typing every repeated value ourselves.
openingTitle: Do We Have to Type Every Entry?
opening: Suppose Botie plans to check three greenhouses on two mornings. We know how many entries the report will need before we know the temperatures. We also want a regular schedule of checks. Neither task should require copying the same number over and over.
NumPy can create arrays from a shape, a repeated value, or a sequence rule. The choice matters: an empty place in a report is not evidence that the thermometer measured zero.

history.title: When the Layout Was Known Before the Measurements
blocks: Scientific programs often know the dimensions of a calculation before they have its results. They need storage for accumulators, trial settings, and numerical grids without writing each entry by hand.

NumPy's array-creation routines make those intentions explicit. A shape describes the arrangement; a fill value or spacing rule describes its initial contents. Our greenhouse schedule is an invented example of that distinction.

intuition.title: Decide what a row means
intuition.explanation: Each row belongs to a morning and each column to a greenhouse.

intuition.title: Choose the initial meaning
intuition.explanation: Zero is appropriate for a count of checks made so far. It is not a replacement for an unmeasured temperature.

intuition.title: Generate the schedule
intuition.explanation: A start, stop, and spacing rule determine which times Botie will inspect.

parts.title: 1. Start With a Shape and a Meaning
paragraphs: For a report with two mornings and three greenhouses, we need two rows and three columns. The shape is a tuple, passed as one argument. zeros fills an array with zeros; ones fills it with ones; full uses a value we supply.

A zero-filled array is useful for a counter before any events have occurred. A constant target table is useful for a shared rule. Neither is a table of observations merely because it has the right shape.

examples.title: Create counts and targets separately
paragraphs: We specify integer storage for counts and floating-point storage for temperatures. The zeros and full functions allocate new arrays.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

checks = np.zeros((2, 3), dtype=int)
targets = np.full((2, 3), 20.0)
print(checks.tolist())
print(targets.tolist())
print(np.ones(3, dtype=int).tolist())
interpretation: The arrays have deliberate initial values. NumPy also offers empty, which leaves numerical contents uninitialised. Those contents must be written before reading them; empty does not mean a safe table of zeros.

parts.title: 2. Reuse a Layout Without Guessing Its Size
paragraphs: Suppose the number of greenhouses changes. Hard-coding three columns in every calculation invites mistakes. The functions ending in _like can take their shape from an existing array. Their default dtype also follows that array, so override it when the new meaning needs a different type.

examples.title: Make a counter that matches the incoming report
paragraphs: Here zeros_like gives each observed position a corresponding counter, and full_like creates a target table with the same layout.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([[12., 18., 24.], [14., 22., 36.]])
counts = np.zeros_like(readings, dtype=int)
targets = np.full_like(readings, 20.0)
print(counts.shape)
print(counts.tolist())
print(targets.tolist())
interpretation: The layout now follows the data. ones_like provides the corresponding all-ones array when every position starts with one contribution.

parts.title: 3. Choose a Step or Choose a Count
paragraphs: A schedule may specify a time interval, while a graph may specify how many points to draw between two limits. Those are different requests. arange uses a step and excludes the stopping boundary. linspace uses a count and includes both endpoints by default.
For fractional spacings, linspace is often clearer when the intended count matters. Floating-point steps in arange can make boundary behaviour surprising.

examples.title: Make an inspection schedule and a trial grid
paragraphs: The first call starts at six, stops before fourteen, and advances by two. The second requests five equally spaced trial settings including zero and one.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

hours = np.arange(6, 14, 2)
settings = np.linspace(0, 1, 5)
print(hours.tolist())
print(settings.tolist())
interpretation: The final argument has a different meaning in these two functions. Treating the count in linspace as a step would give the wrong experiment.

parts.title: 4. Preserve a Measurement When No Change Is Intended
paragraphs: Later we will use matrices to combine measurements. We also need a matrix that expresses leaving each measurement alone. An identity matrix has ones on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere, so each output keeps its matching input and ignores the others.

title: Choose the Readings Without Losing Their Place
blurb: Botie may need one morning, a run of mornings, or selected greenhouses. We need to express each request precisely and know whether editing the selection will change the original report.
openingTitle: Which Part of the Report Did We Ask For?
opening: A report with hundreds of rows is useful only if we can retrieve the observations we need. Sometimes they are adjacent. Sometimes we need particular positions in a particular order. Those requests should not be confused.

We will follow a small temperature table through slices and explicit index selections, then check which results share storage with the original. This matters whenever we prepare data while keeping the original measurements available.

history.title: Working on Part of a Large Scientific Record
blocks: Scientific arrays can be too large to copy every time a calculation needs a subset. Regular stretches of storage can often be described by a starting position, a length, and a step.

NumPy distinguishes basic slicing, which can share storage, from advanced indexing, which gathers values into a new array. Those documented rules explain both the convenience of selection and the need for care when editing it.

intuition.title: Keep the original order visible
intuition.explanation: Rows are mornings; columns are north, middle, south.

intuition.title: A range follows existing positions
intuition.explanation: Taking the first two mornings keeps their order and stops before the third.

intuition.title: A gather follows requested positions

parts.title: 1. Read a Slice From Start to Stop
paragraphs: A slice has a start, a stop, and an optional step. The stop is excluded. Leaving a boundary empty uses the corresponding end of the axis. A negative index counts back from the end, so minus one selects the last entry.
In a matrix we supply a selector for each axis, separated by a comma. Selecting with a single integer removes that axis; selecting a one-entry slice keeps it.

examples.title: Keep a row, or keep a one-row table
paragraphs: These selections contain the same first-day readings, but the resulting shapes differ. The last expression selects every other greenhouse from the final day.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([[10,20,30],[14,22,36],[16,24,38]])
print(a[0].tolist())
print(a[0].shape)
print(a[0:1].shape)
print(a[-1, ::2].tolist())
interpretation: Keeping an axis can make a later calculation easier to align. The step of two selects columns zero and two; it does not multiply the temperatures.

parts.title: 2. Choose Positions in an Explicit Order
paragraphs: An integer index array requests positions rather than a continuous range. It can reorder entries or repeat them. For multiple axes, two index lists normally identify pairs of coordinates. If we want every combination of chosen rows and chosen columns, we need to express that different request.

examples.title: Pairs of coordinates or a rectangular selection
paragraphs: The paired request retrieves row two, column one and row zero, column two. ix_ creates selectors for all combinations of those row and column choices.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([[10,20,30],[14,22,36],[16,24,38]])
print(a[[2, 0]].tolist())
print(a[[2, 0], [1, 2]].tolist())
print(a[np.ix_([2, 0], [1, 2])].tolist())
interpretation: The rectangle has two selected rows and two selected columns. Pairwise selection has only two entries. Neither operation is a mistake by itself; they answer different questions.

parts.title: 3. Decide Whether an Edit Should Reach the Original
paragraphs: A name is not a copy. Assigning a second name to an array gives both names the same object. A basic slice also shares the underlying numerical storage. An advanced selection gathers into independent storage. Use copy when independence is part of the task.

examples.title: Inspect sharing before editing
paragraphs: shares_memory reports whether these arrays overlap in memory. A slice and an integer-index selection can show the same values while behaving differently when changed.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([10, 20, 30])
view = a[:2]
gathered = a[[0, 1]]
independent = a.copy()
print(np.shares_memory(a, view))
print(np.shares_memory(a, gathered))
view[0] = 11
gathered[1] = 99
print(a.tolist())
print(independent.tolist())
interpretation: The slice changed the original first reading. The gathered array and explicit copy did not. np.asarray is useful for accepting an input as an array, but it may return an existing array unchanged; it is not a promise to make a copy.

parts.title: 4. Count Repeated Positions Deliberately
paragraphs: Repeated retrieval is straightforward, but repeated updates need care. When advanced indexing gathers a temporary array, an in-place-looking update can lose repeated contributions. If every occurrence should add to a count, NumPy's add.at performs an update at each supplied position.

examples.title: Two alerts for the same greenhouse
paragraphs: Our saved alert IDs contain greenhouse one twice. We compare an indexed increment with accumulation that processes every occurrence.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

ids = np.array([1, 1, 2])
buffered = np.zeros(3, dtype=int)
buffered[ids] += 1
counts = np.zeros(3, dtype=int)
np.add.at(counts, ids, 1)
print(buffered.tolist())
print(counts.tolist())
interpretation: The second result records all three alerts. This distinction will matter when later lessons accumulate repeated token IDs or category observations.

title: Put the Same Readings Into the Right Arrangement
blurb: A sensor may send one long sequence while a calculation expects rows. We need to change the arrangement without changing which measurements belong to each day and greenhouse.
openingTitle: Where Does One Day End and the Next Begin?
opening: Botie's logger sends six readings in order: all three greenhouses on Monday, then all three on Tuesday. The message has no row breaks. We need to restore the table before asking for a daily or greenhouse summary.

Reshaping changes how existing entries are grouped. Transposing exchanges axes. Joining combines separate collections. These operations can produce similar-looking shapes while assigning very different meanings to their positions.

prerequisites.title: Choose the Readings Without Losing Their Place

history.title: Separating Stored Order From the Shape of a Calculation
blocks: Scientific instruments and file formats often deliver observations in a flat sequence. Numerical calculations need arrangements that identify time, location, and measurement channels.

NumPy's manipulation routines describe shape and axis changes explicitly. This makes array-oriented calculations possible without treating every change of layout as a new measurement. The documented distinction between reshape, transpose, and joining is the mechanism we use here.

intuition.title: Read the logger's order
intuition.explanation: The first three values belong to Monday and the next three to Tuesday.

intuition.title: Restore the day boundary
intuition.explanation: Group consecutive triples into day rows.

intuition.title: Then follow a greenhouse instead
intuition.explanation: Swapping axes puts each greenhouse's two readings together.

parts.title: 1. Restore Boundaries With reshape
paragraphs: The default reshape order reads the original entries in row order and puts them into the requested row order. It cannot create or discard entries. The product of the new dimensions must match the number of existing entries.
One dimension may be minus one, meaning infer this length from the remaining dimensions and the number of entries. It does not mean a missing observation.

examples.title: Recover two days from six readings
paragraphs: We know that each day contains three readings, so either give both dimensions or let NumPy infer the day count.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

flat = np.array([10,20,30,14,22,36])
days = flat.reshape(2, 3)
print(days.tolist())
print(flat.reshape(-1, 3).shape)
print(days.ravel().tolist())
interpretation: ravel returns a flat array in row order. It can return a view or a copy depending on the layout. flatten always copies. Neither operation recovers labels that were never stored.

parts.title: 2. Exchange Axes With Transpose
paragraphs: Regrouping the sequence into three pairs is not the same as following each greenhouse across days. A transpose exchanges the roles of rows and columns while keeping each value attached to its original coordinates.
The T attribute is a convenient transpose for a matrix. On arrays with more axes, name the intended axis order explicitly rather than assuming that reversing all axes is what the task needs.

examples.title: Compare a reshape with an axis exchange
paragraphs: Both outputs below have three rows and two columns. Inspect their values to see why shape alone cannot establish meaning.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

days = np.array([[10,20,30],[14,22,36]])
print(days.reshape(3, 2).tolist())
print(days.T.tolist())
interpretation: Only the transpose places the north greenhouse's two readings together, then the middle's, then the south's. reshape has no knowledge of greenhouse identity.

parts.title: 3. Add Observations or Add an Axis
paragraphs: concatenate extends an existing axis. stack creates a new axis to keep its inputs separate. Suppose we have two daily vectors. Concatenating them makes a longer vector; stacking them makes a table of days.
When joining tables, all dimensions other than the concatenation axis must match. When stacking, the input shapes must match because each becomes a slice along the new axis.

examples.title: Keep the day boundary when combining reports
paragraphs: We stack two same-length vectors into rows, then append a third row to the resulting table. The third day's extra brackets preserve its row axis.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

monday = np.array([10,20,30])
tuesday = np.array([14,22,36])
print(np.concatenate([monday, tuesday]).shape)
days = np.stack([monday, tuesday], axis=0)
print(days.tolist())
wednesday = np.array([[16,24,38]])
print(np.concatenate([days, wednesday], axis=0).tolist())
interpretation: The first operation discards the day boundary unless we record it elsewhere. The last operation extends an existing day axis.

parts.title: 4. Keep Features and Batches Distinct
paragraphs: A model often receives a table with observations in rows and features in columns. column_stack turns equally long vectors into feature columns. A batch adds another meaning: a group of observations processed together.
When there are three or more axes, write down what each one means before manipulating the shape. Equal lengths do not make two axes interchangeable.

examples.title: Build feature columns, then preserve a batch axis
paragraphs: Here each row describes a greenhouse. We keep temperature and humidity in separate columns. expand_dims introduces a new axis of length one; squeeze removes a named axis only if its length is one.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

temperature = np.array([12., 18., 24.])
humidity = np.array([50., 60., 70.])
features = np.column_stack([temperature, humidity])
batch = np.expand_dims(features, axis=0)
print(features.tolist())
print(batch.shape)
print(np.squeeze(batch, axis=0).shape)
interpretation: The batch shape means one batch, three observations, and two features. Specifying the squeeze axis avoids accidentally removing other meaningful length-one axes.

title: One Reference for Many Rows
blurb: Each greenhouse has its own target temperature. We want to compare every day's readings with those three targets without copying the targets into a new table by hand.
openingTitle: Do We Need to Repeat the Same Reference Every Day?
opening: Suppose the north, middle, and south greenhouses have target temperatures of 10, 20, and 30 degrees. Botie checks them on two days. Each day needs the same three references, in the same order.
We could write those targets beside every row. Instead, we can tell the array calculation that this one target row applies to every day. NumPy calls this matching of compatible shapes broadcasting.

history.title: Repeating a Calculation Without Repeating Its Data
blocks: Array calculations often combine a large collection with a smaller reference: one scale for all entries, or one target for each feature column. Explicitly constructing a second large table adds work and obscures that the reference is shared.

NumPy's broadcasting rules specify when smaller shapes can be reused across larger ones. Our greenhouse example illustrates one such case. It is not a claim that NumPy understands the meaning of the columns; matching the references to the right columns remains our responsibility.

intuition.title: Start with two days of readings
intuition.explanation: The greenhouse order is north, middle, south in every row.

intuition.title: Supply one target per greenhouse
intuition.explanation: The target belongs to a column. It does not change with the day.

intuition.title: Keep a difference for every reading
intuition.explanation: Positive means above target; negative means below target. We still have both days and all three greenhouses.

parts.title: 1. Match the Reference to Its Meaning
paragraphs: Each greenhouse needs its own target. We could keep those three targets as a one-dimensional array, as one row of a table, or as three rows with one column. Those arrangements contain the same numbers, but they do not tell NumPy to align them in the same way.
A one-dimensional array has positions along one axis. It has no separate row and column axes, even though printing it may put the entries on one line.
interpretation: Let's make all three arrangements explicitly before deciding which one belongs beside our readings.

examples.title: The same values in three different shapes
paragraphs: A flat list creates one axis. A list containing one inner list creates one row. Three inner lists containing one item each create three rows and one column. Printing the shapes makes this distinction visible.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

targets = np.array([10, 20, 30])
target_row = np.array([[10, 20, 30]])
target_column = np.array([[10], [20], [30]])

print(targets.shape)
print(target_row.shape)
print(target_column.shape)
print(target_row.tolist())
print(target_column.tolist())
interpretation: Our greenhouse targets belong to the columns of the readings table. Both the one-dimensional target array and the one-row version can align those three entries with the three columns. The column version would arrange them along the wrong direction for this example.

parts.title: 2. Subtract the Same Targets From Every Day
paragraphs: We want each target to stay with its greenhouse as Botie moves from Monday to Tuesday. That means subtracting the first target from the first greenhouse on both days, then doing the same for the other greenhouses.
interpretation: A positive difference means the reading was above target; a negative difference means it was below. We still need a difference for every reading.

examples.title: Keep the reference array small
paragraphs: The subtraction below reuses the targets for both rows. This is broadcasting: NumPy aligns compatible shapes so an operation can use a smaller input across a larger one. We do not need to write a second copy of the targets.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([
    [12, 18, 24],
    [14, 22, 36],
])
targets = np.array([10, 20, 30])
differences = readings - targets

print(differences.tolist())
print(differences.shape)
interpretation: The two day rows and three greenhouse columns survive. Broadcasting has reused a reference, not combined observations into a summary.

parts.title: 3. Read the Shape Rule From the Right
paragraphs: NumPy compares axis lengths starting from the right of each shape. Two lengths can work together if they match or if one is one. A missing leading axis acts like an axis of length one. This lets our three targets apply to both day rows.

Now suppose the reference is the outside temperature for each day. Each reference must apply across a whole row. We therefore need two rows with one entry each. A flat two-entry array would instead try to align with our three greenhouse columns.
parts.calculation:
Greenhouse targets: (2, 3) with    (3,) → (2, 3)
Day references:     (2, 3) with (2, 1) → (2, 3)
Wrong alignment:    (2, 3) with    (2,) → incompatible
interpretation: The computer checks the lengths, not the meaning. A square table can conceal an alignment mistake because its row and column counts happen to match.

examples.title: Give each day's reference a column axis
paragraphs: We already used a colon to keep all positions along an axis. In the indexing expression below, None adds a new axis of length one. It does not insert an unknown temperature. The comma separates these two indexing instructions.
We keep the two day entries, give them a one-column axis, and inspect the result before subtracting. These illustrative outside readings differ from the ones you will use in the challenge.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([
    [12, 18, 24],
    [14, 22, 36],
])
outside = np.array([6, 10])
outside_column = outside[:, None]

print(outside.shape)
print(outside_column.shape)
print(outside_column.tolist())
print((readings - outside_column).tolist())
interpretation: The first outside temperature now aligns with Monday and the second with Tuesday. Adding the axis gives a new view of the same two stored values. It does not copy either temperature three times.

examples.title: A square table can accept the wrong interpretation
paragraphs: Both the day count and greenhouse count are two here. Subtracting a flat outside array therefore succeeds, but applies the two references to columns. Adding the one-column axis instead attaches them to days.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([[12,18],[14,22]])
outside = np.array([6,10])
print((readings - outside).tolist())
print((readings - outside[:, None]).tolist())
interpretation: Both outputs have the same shape. Only the second uses each day's outside reading across that day's whole row. Understanding the input meaning is still necessary after a program stops reporting shape errors.

parts.title: 4. Keep Reuse Separate From Reduction
paragraphs: Subtracting a target and averaging the resulting differences answer two different questions. The subtraction asks how far each reading is from its target. The average asks for a summary across several readings.
Follow the shapes as well as the values. Broadcasting can preserve our table, whereas a reduction combines entries along the axis we name.
interpretation: The workshop asks for the full table of differences. This next example goes a step further to show what would happen if Botie also requested one summary per greenhouse.

examples.title: One table of differences, then one summary per column
paragraphs: We subtract first, then average over days. The first shape still describes a day-by-greenhouse table. The second describes one entry per greenhouse.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([[12, 18, 24], [14, 22, 36]])
targets = np.array([10, 20, 30])
differences = readings - targets
average_difference = differences.mean(axis=0)

print(differences.shape)
print(average_difference.shape)
print(average_difference.tolist())
interpretation: An average difference of zero does not tell us that every reading was on target. Above-target and below-target readings can cancel. Keep the individual differences when that distinction matters.

title: Ask Each Row a Question
blurb: Botie needs the greenhouse readings that reached a temperature limit. A yes-or-no decision for each reading lets us select the relevant observations without losing their order.
openingTitle: Which Readings Need Our Attention?
opening: A greenhouse report includes comfortable temperatures and readings that need attention. We want to see only the readings at or above 25 degrees, while keeping the original collection available.
We can ask the same question of every entry. The answers form another array, containing true or false at each position. This array of decisions is called a mask.

history.title: Selecting Observations Without Rewriting the Table

sources.title: Python: lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries

blocks: Selecting observations is a recurring problem in scientific computing: a calculation might need only a certain period, a particular group, or measurements that satisfy a condition. Keeping a decision beside each observation separates the selection rule from the stored measurements.

NumPy documents Boolean indexing as a way to use those decisions. This lesson uses invented greenhouse readings to show the mechanism. It teaches selection, not a claim that all unusual observations should be discarded.

intuition.title: Keep the full report
intuition.explanation: Each position belongs to one greenhouse reading. The threshold includes the boundary itself.

intuition.title: Ask the same question four times
intuition.explanation: A true decision means this reading meets the rule. It is a selection instruction, not a replacement temperature.

parts.title: 1. Build One Decision per Observation
paragraphs: Botie needs to know which greenhouses have readings at or above the alert temperature. We could inspect each reading ourselves, but a program needs an explicit decision rule. A comparison asks a question about a value and returns a Boolean: either True or False.

Applying the comparison to an array produces another array with a Boolean at each position. This array of decisions is called a mask. Its entries answer whether to keep a reading; they are not temperatures.
interpretation: Our boundary counts. A strictly greater-than comparison would omit the reading exactly at the threshold.

examples.title: Compare once, then compare at every position
paragraphs: The Python operator below means greater than or equal to. First we use it on one number, then on an array. The array's dtype is bool because the stored entries are decisions.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

print(27 >= 25)
readings = np.array([20, 27, 25, 18])
mask = readings >= 25

print(mask.tolist())
print(mask.dtype)
print(mask.shape)
interpretation: The mask has four entries because there are four readings to decide about. We have only created the decisions so far. The original temperatures are still in readings.

parts.title: 2. Use the Decisions to Select Values
paragraphs: We now have two aligned collections: the temperatures and the decisions. Putting the Boolean mask inside the readings' square brackets tells NumPy to keep the positions marked True. For this one-dimensional selection, the mask must have one decision per reading.

A Boolean mask and an array of integer indices are different structures for making a selection. The Boolean array asks yes or no at each position. The integer array names the positions to retrieve, in the order requested.
interpretation: The workshop displays decisions as zero and one. In NumPy we must actually use Boolean values for a mask. A numerical array containing zeros and ones would instead be interpreted as positions.

examples.title: Decisions are different from numbered positions
paragraphs: Both selections below are valid Python, but only the first applies our alert rule. In the second, each zero requests the first reading and each one requests the second reading.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([20, 27, 25, 18])
mask = np.array([False, True, True, False])
positions = np.array([0, 1, 1, 0])

print(readings[mask].tolist())
print(readings[positions].tolist())
interpretation: The mask selects two readings. The index array retrieves four entries, including repeats. Using the right values with the wrong data type can therefore ask an entirely different question.

parts.title: 3. Summarise the Selected Group
paragraphs: After selecting the readings, we can count them or calculate their average. Both the total and the count must come from the selected group. The original report's count would give us the wrong denominator.
parts.calculation:
Selected total = 27 + 25 = 52
Selected count = 2
Selected mean = 52 / 2 = 26
interpretation: An empty selection still has a count of zero, but it has no mean. There are no temperatures to average, so a displayed zero would wrongly suggest an observed temperature.

examples.title: The selection is another numerical array
paragraphs: The selected array has the same numerical data type as the readings. It can have fewer entries, so inspect its size before treating it as the whole report.

In the last print, an f before a quoted string lets us put an expression inside braces. Python evaluates the expression before the colon. The .1f after the colon asks for its value with one digit after the decimal point.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([20, 27, 25, 18])
selected = readings[readings >= 25]

print(selected.tolist())
print(selected.size)
print(f"{selected.mean():.1f}")
interpretation: The list shows which observations contributed. The next line counts them, and the last summarises them. Boolean selection here creates a copy, so changing this selected array later would not edit readings.

examples.title: Keep an empty result distinguishable from a measured zero
paragraphs: On this cooler day, no reading meets the rule. The result is still an array, just one with no entries. The if statement chooses what to do when the count is zero. The double equals sign compares two values; it does not assign a value to a name.
examples.code:

selected = readings[readings >= 25]

print(selected.tolist())
print(selected.shape)
if selected.size == 0:
    print("No readings met the alert rule.")
else:
    print(selected.mean())

(0,)
No readings met the alert rule.
interpretation: The empty list display and the zero-length shape both say that no items were selected. The indented instruction under if runs when the comparison is true; the instruction under else runs otherwise. We never ask for an average of the empty array.

parts.title: 4. A Filter Changes the Question
paragraphs: The mean of readings above the limit does not describe the whole report without qualification. We deliberately chose warmer readings. That is useful for inspecting alerts, but someone reading the result needs to know which observations contributed.

Another Python structure, the set, keeps distinct items. It is useful when we care whether a value occurred, but it discards repeated occurrences and does not give us positions to index like a list. That would lose information if we used it to store repeated measurements.
interpretation: Let's distinguish asking which temperatures occurred from asking how many readings triggered an alert.

examples.title: Distinct temperatures are not the same as individual readings
paragraphs: These are three separate alert readings, two of which happen to have the same value. Constructing a set keeps that value only once. We use sorted to produce a list for predictable display; the set itself has no sequence order to rely on. The in operator checks membership.
examples.code:
alert_readings = [27, 27, 25]
distinct_temperatures = set(alert_readings)

print(len(alert_readings))
print(sorted(distinct_temperatures))
print(len(distinct_temperatures))
print(27 in distinct_temperatures)
interpretation: There were three readings but only two distinct temperatures. A set is appropriate for the second question. Keep the list or numerical array for calculations in which each observation should count.

title: Summarise a Report Without Losing the Question
blurb: Botie needs totals, typical readings, and the greenhouse that needs attention first. A value, a position, and an ordered report answer different questions, even when they come from the same array.
openingTitle: Do We Need the Hottest Reading or the Greenhouse That Produced It?
opening: A maximum temperature tells Botie how hot a greenhouse became. It does not by itself identify which greenhouse to inspect. An average answers another question, and an average alone can hide a large spread.
We will calculate these summaries with NumPy, keep their axis meanings explicit, and use returned positions to preserve the connection between values and labels.

history.title: Turning a Large Report Into a Specific Answer
blocks: Scientists needed summaries long before NumPy: totals, central values, and measures of variation compress observations into answers to particular questions. Array libraries must make clear which observations each summary combines.

NumPy's statistical reductions accept axes, while functions such as argmax return positions instead of measurements. Keeping that distinction explicit lets a numerical summary remain connected to its original observation.

intuition.title: Keep labels beside readings
intuition.explanation: The order is north, middle, south, annex.

intuition.title: A value and its position are different answers
intuition.explanation: The highest reading is attached to position one in the supplied order.

intuition.explanation: Sorting the readings alone would detach them from their greenhouse names.

parts.title: 1. Choose the Summary and the Axis
paragraphs: sum adds values; mean shares their total across the entries; min and max keep an extreme value. Each can reduce a selected axis. The keepdims argument retains a length-one version of the reduced axis, which makes the result easier to align with the original table.

examples.title: Subtract each day's own average
paragraphs: We preserve the greenhouse axis as length one in the daily mean. Broadcasting can then subtract each day's reference from its whole row.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

days = np.array([[10.,20.,30.],[14.,22.,36.]])
daily_mean = days.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
print(days.sum(axis=0).tolist())
print(daily_mean.tolist())
print((days - daily_mean).tolist())
interpretation: Keeping the axis does not change the average. It records where that average belongs when we reuse it.

parts.title: 2. Describe the Centre and the Spread
paragraphs: A mean describes a centre; variance and standard deviation describe spread around it. NumPy's default variance divides squared deviations by the number of entries. Setting ddof to one instead uses one fewer in the divisor, the usual sample-variance convention when estimating from a sample.

The median selects the middle of ordered observations, averaging the two middle values for an even count. Quantiles locate other fractions of the ordered data. Their interpolation rule matters for small samples; we use NumPy's default linear rule here.

examples.title: Keep the convention beside the result
paragraphs: For these four readings, compare the population variance, sample variance, and middle half of the ordered values.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([18.,20.,25.,27.])
print(readings.mean())
print(np.median(readings))
print(readings.var())
print(np.round(readings.var(ddof=1), 4))
print(np.round(readings.std(), 4))
print(np.quantile(readings, [0.25, 0.75]).tolist())
interpretation: The two variance results use different denominators on the same observations. Choose the convention for the question, rather than changing ddof until a desired number appears. Standard deviation returns to the original temperature units.

parts.title: 3. Retrieve the Observation Behind an Extreme
paragraphs: max returns the largest value. argmax returns its position. If values tie, argmax returns the first occurrence along the chosen axis. The position can retrieve a greenhouse name or a complete record.
argsort returns all positions in sorted order. Apply that same order to every aligned array. np.sort returns sorted values instead; the array's sort method sorts that array in place.

examples.title: Move names and readings together
paragraphs: We request a stable sort so ties keep their original order. These readings are distinct, but making the rule explicit prevents ambiguity later.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

names = np.array(["north","middle","south","annex"])
readings = np.array([20,27,25,18])
print(readings.max())
print(readings.argmax())
print(names[readings.argmax()])
order = np.argsort(readings, kind="stable")
print(names[order].tolist())
print(readings[order].tolist())
interpretation: The index array carries the ordering rule to both collections. Sorting each collection independently would destroy the measurement-to-name relationship.

parts.title: 4. Count Decisions and Repeated Values
paragraphs: A Boolean comparison can be summarised too. count_nonzero counts true entries, any asks whether at least one is true, and all asks whether every entry is true. Use those operations to reduce an array of decisions to one answer.

unique can return distinct values together with their counts. Its usual sorted result differs from preserving the first occurrence order. Later, category IDs must use a vocabulary whose ordering we deliberately maintain.

examples.title: How many alerts, and which values repeated?
paragraphs: The alert comparison includes the boundary. Tuple unpacking gives the two returned arrays separate names: values and counts.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([20,27,27,18])
alerts = readings >= 25
print(np.count_nonzero(alerts))
print(alerts.any())
print(alerts.all())
values, counts = np.unique(readings, return_counts=True)
print(values.tolist())
print(counts.tolist())
interpretation: There are two alert observations, even though both have the same value. Counting distinct alert temperatures would answer a different question.

title: One Calculation for a Whole Report
blurb: Botie applies the same rule to many readings. We will first write the repeated steps, then express them with array operations while keeping the intermediate values and memory costs understandable.
openingTitle: How Do We Repeat a Rule Without Hiding What It Does?
opening: Suppose we need to compare every greenhouse reading with a target. A Python loop can visit each entry, subtract the target, and save the result. Once we understand those steps, an array expression can ask NumPy to perform that same repeated calculation.

This is vectorisation. It is useful because common numerical loops can run inside compiled library routines, but a short expression is not automatically correct or economical. We still need to understand the operations and the shapes it creates.

history.title: Moving Repeated Arithmetic Into Numerical Routines
blocks: Scientific Python programs often repeat a small arithmetic rule over many observations. Performing each iteration through Python has overhead, while compiled array routines can carry out many such operations directly.

NumPy exposes common elementwise operations as universal functions, often shortened to ufuncs. This lets us express the numerical rule at array scale. It does not eliminate the need to inspect temporary arrays or prove that the rule matches the intended calculation.

intuition.title: Start with observations and a reference
intuition.explanation: Each greenhouse is compared with the same target.

intuition.title: Keep one difference per observation
intuition.explanation: Subtracting gives direction as well as size.

intuition.title: Then decide how to summarise error
intuition.explanation: Squaring makes negative and positive deviations contribute positively.

parts.title: 1. Follow the Repeated Steps Before Shortening Them
paragraphs: A for statement visits each value in a collection. The indented instructions run for the current value, then repeat for the next. We can append each result to an initially empty list.
An array subtraction performs the corresponding elementwise operation. Elementwise means each output is calculated from the corresponding input entry or aligned entries.

examples.title: The loop and the array expression answer the same question
paragraphs: The loop version makes the repeated operation visible. The array version expresses that rule for the collection.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([18,22,26])
differences = []
for reading in readings:
    differences.append(int(reading - 20))
print(differences)
print((readings - 20).tolist())
interpretation: int converts each scalar to a Python integer for the list display. The shorter form avoids our explicit Python loop. np.vectorize can make a Python function convenient to call over arrays, but it is not a promise of compiled-loop speed.

parts.title: 2. Combine Elementwise Steps With a Reduction
paragraphs: The size of an error and its direction answer different questions. abs discards the sign. square squares each entry. sqrt takes square roots. Reducing afterwards, with mean for example, combines the separate contributions.
Keep intermediate arrays named while learning the calculation. That makes it possible to check whether a sign was lost too soon or a reduction happened along the wrong axis.

examples.title: Calculate error contributions before averaging them
paragraphs: These residuals are observations minus a target. We print each transformation before reporting the average squared error and its square root.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

residuals = np.array([18.,22.,26.]) - 20
squared = np.square(residuals)
print(np.abs(residuals).tolist())
print(squared.tolist())
print(np.round(squared.mean(), 4))
print(np.round(np.sqrt(squared.mean()), 4))
interpretation: Squaring prevents opposite signs from cancelling. Taking a square root after averaging returns to the original units; averaging square roots would be a different calculation.

parts.title: 3. Choose Between Values Without Dropping Positions
paragraphs: A Boolean mask selects a subset and can shorten an array. where instead chooses one of two values at each position, preserving the aligned output shape. Its arguments are a condition, the value when true, and the value when false.

Use parentheses around each array comparison when combining them with & for and, | for or, and ~ for not. Python's plain and and or expect single truth decisions and are not substitutes for these elementwise operators.

examples.title: Keep a report while marking readings inside a band
paragraphs: The mask identifies readings inside our illustrative operating band. where writes a label at every original position, while Boolean indexing keeps only qualifying readings.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([18,22,26])
inside = (readings >= 20) & (readings <= 25)
print(inside.tolist())
print(np.where(inside, "within band", "review").tolist())
print(readings[inside].tolist())
interpretation: The labels still correspond to all three original readings. The selected list contains only one. A condition does not need to mean deletion.

parts.title: 4. Use a Named Operation When It Expresses the Rule
paragraphs: maximum can compare each entry with a lower bound; minimum can compare with an upper bound; clip applies both limits. These operations change values rather than filtering observations. Preserve the original if the clipped values are only intended for a display.

Other ufuncs used later include exp and log for exponential and logarithmic calculations, and sin and cos for angles in radians. Their input assumptions matter: a real logarithm needs a positive value, and a negative value has no real square root.

examples.title: Limit the display without rewriting the sensor reading
paragraphs: The clipped result puts every displayed entry inside the requested range. It does not establish that the sensor's out-of-range reading was wrong.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([18,22,26])
display = np.clip(readings, 20, 25)
print(display.tolist())
print(readings.tolist())
ratios = np.array([1.,2.,4.])
print(np.round(np.exp(np.log(ratios)), 6).tolist())
interpretation: The original readings are unchanged. The final line illustrates reversing a logarithmic transformation for positive ratios, subject to floating-point precision. It is not a reason to logarithmically transform every temperature report.

parts.title: 5. Check the Arrays a Short Expression Creates
paragraphs: Broadcasting can create a large output even when both inputs are modest. Comparing every observation with every reference can produce a three-dimensional intermediate: observation, reference, feature. A batch reduces how many observations we handle at once.

The nbytes attribute reports an array's numerical storage size. A copy and a view can expose equal nbytes even when the view shares storage, so it is not the total unique memory used by a whole program. Profile real workloads before making speed claims.

examples.title: Count storage before scaling the example
paragraphs: Each float64 entry uses eight bytes. The new axis below creates a view; square creates a numerical result array.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([[18.,22.,26.],[19.,23.,27.]])
print(readings.nbytes)
expanded = readings[:, None, :]
print(expanded.shape)
print(np.shares_memory(readings, expanded))
print(np.square(readings).shape)
interpretation: Know which axes and temporary results an expression introduces before applying it to millions of records. Vectorisation is a way to express repeated work, not a guarantee that all work fits in memory.

title: Turn Several Measurements Into Several Predictions
blurb: A prediction can combine temperature and humidity with separate coefficients. Matrix operations let us apply that same rule to every greenhouse, then check how a fitted rule relates to its observations.
openingTitle: How Can One Rule Read a Whole Table?
opening: Botie has two measurements for every greenhouse. A simple illustrative score gives each measurement a coefficient, adds its contributions, then adds an offset. We can calculate one greenhouse's score by hand before doing the same for a whole table.

This is where the distinction between elementwise multiplication and matrix multiplication matters. We will keep the observations, feature columns, coefficients, and output shapes visible at every step.

prerequisites.title: One Calculation for a Whole Report

history.title: Reusing Numerical Linear Algebra for Many Observations
blocks: Solving systems of equations and fitting more equations than there are unknowns are longstanding numerical problems. Reliable implementations need algorithms that account for rounding and the structure of the system.

NumPy's linear algebra interface draws on established BLAS and LAPACK routines. We use that interface after making the small matrix calculation visible, and distinguish solving an exact square system from fitting an overdetermined one.

intuition.title: Keep one observation per row
intuition.explanation: These are invented temperature and humidity features.

intuition.title: Give each feature a contribution rule
intuition.explanation: The same coefficients apply to every row.

intuition.title: Sum within each observation
intuition.explanation: The resulting scores stay in north, south order.

parts.title: 1. Inspect the Contributions Before Summing
paragraphs: Elementwise multiplication combines matching entries without adding them. A dot product multiplies matching entries and then adds those products. For one observation, the feature and coefficient vectors must have equal lengths.
The coefficients in this example are supplied solely to illustrate the calculation. They are not a trained rule or a physical greenhouse control law.

examples.title: Calculate one greenhouse's score
paragraphs: The temperature contributes through its own coefficient, and humidity through another. We print those contributions before the sum and the offset.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

features = np.array([10.,40.])
weights = np.array([2.,0.1])
contributions = features * weights
print(contributions.tolist())
print(np.dot(features, weights))
print(np.dot(features, weights) + 3)
interpretation: The elementwise product has two entries. The dot product reduces them to one weighted sum. Adding the offset completes the score.

parts.title: 2. Apply the Same Rule to Every Row
paragraphs: The @ operator performs matrix multiplication. For a two-dimensional feature table and a one-dimensional coefficient vector, it computes one dot product per row. The feature count must match the coefficient count.
For matrix times matrix, the left matrix's column count must match the right matrix's row count. The surviving outer dimensions describe the output.

examples.title: Keep one prediction per greenhouse
paragraphs: Our table has two observations and two features. Multiplying by a two-entry coefficient vector leaves one score per observation. Multiplying by the identity leaves the feature table unchanged.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[10.,40.],[20.,60.]])
weights = np.array([2.,0.1])
scores = X @ weights + 3
print(scores.tolist())
print(scores.shape)
print((X @ np.eye(2)).tolist())
interpretation: Using X * weights would instead leave a contribution for each feature, with two columns still present. It is useful intermediate data, but it is not the same result as @.

parts.title: 3. Check Distance With a Norm
paragraphs: A norm measures the size of a vector. The Euclidean norm squares its coordinates, adds them, and takes the square root. np.linalg.norm performs this calculation; naming an axis lets us calculate it separately for each row.
When coordinates are different kinds of measurement, a raw distance can be dominated by their units. Later scaling lessons explain how to make such comparisons meaningful.

examples.title: One length for each error vector
paragraphs: These invented vectors are already on comparable scales. Reducing along the feature axis gives one length for each observation.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

errors = np.array([[3.,4.],[0.,5.]])
print(np.linalg.norm(errors, axis=1).tolist())
print(np.sqrt(np.square(errors).sum(axis=1)).tolist())
interpretation: The second expression exposes the steps performed by the norm. Its five-unit result describes length, not an average coordinate error.

parts.title: 4. Solve an Exact System Before Fitting an Approximation
paragraphs: If a square coefficient matrix has an independent constraint for each unknown, solve can find values satisfying that system. Do not explicitly compute an inverse merely to apply it to one right-hand side. A singular matrix does not supply a unique solution.

With more observations than unknowns, exact agreement may be impossible. lstsq finds coefficients minimising the sum of squared residuals. It also returns information about the fit and the rank, the number of independent directions supported by the matrix.

examples.title: Recover two settings and check the equations
paragraphs: The supplied equations require the sum of two settings to be thirty and their difference to be ten. We check the computed solution by putting it back into the equations.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1.,1.],[1.,-1.]])
b = np.array([30.,10.])
settings = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print(settings.tolist())
print((A @ settings).tolist())
interpretation: Recomputing the left-hand side confirms what the settings do. Floating-point systems generally need a tolerance check, which the numerical-checks lesson will introduce.

examples.title: Fit a line when there are more observations than coefficients
paragraphs: The first column is all ones for the intercept; the second is the input. lstsq returns four items, which we unpack into separate names. We will inspect the coefficients, predictions, and rank.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([0.,1.,2.])
y = np.array([1.,2.,2.])
X = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x])
weights, residual_sums, rank, singular_values = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
print(np.round(weights, 4).tolist())
print(np.round(X @ weights, 4).tolist())
print(rank)
interpretation: The line cannot pass through all three observations. It balances their squared residuals. The returned residual_sums is not the array of individual errors; calculate those from predictions and observations when you need to inspect them. Near-dependent features can make fitted coefficients sensitive even when the program returns a result.

title: When Two Calculations Almost Agree
blurb: A tiny rounding difference, a missing observation, and a wrongly shaped result are different problems. We need checks that distinguish them before trusting a numerical answer.
openingTitle: Did the Method Fail, or Did We Ask the Wrong Check?
opening: Botie converts a report, then reverses the conversion to check the original readings. The recovered numbers may differ by a tiny rounding amount. An exact comparison can reject a perfectly useful calculation, but accepting every small-looking difference would also be careless.
We need to choose what agreement means for the task. That includes the arrangement of the result, the kind of numbers it stores, whether its entries are finite, and how much numerical error we allow.

prerequisites.title: One Calculation for a Whole Report

history.title: Representing Real Quantities With Finite Storage
blocks: A computer has a finite number of bits for each stored numerical value. Many decimal fractions therefore cannot be represented exactly in binary floating-point storage. Repeated arithmetic must round intermediate results.

NumPy exposes data types, finite-value checks, and approximate comparisons so a program can account for those limitations. The tolerance is part of our numerical contract, not a way to declare every discrepancy harmless.

intuition.title: Keep the expected result
intuition.explanation: We want a converted reading to match its reference closely.

intuition.title: State an allowed difference
intuition.explanation: An absolute tolerance is measured in the result's own units.

intuition.title: Check the whole contract
intuition.explanation: Agreement includes layout and usable values, not only a similar printed number.

parts.title: 1. Choose Storage Before Losing Information
paragraphs: The dtype controls the representation used for every entry in an ordinary numerical array. Assigning a fraction into integer storage discards its fractional part. Converting the array afterwards cannot recover information that has already been lost.

Fixed-width integer types also have limits, unlike Python's arbitrary-precision integers. Choose a type that can represent the required range. Narrowing a type merely to save memory can change the calculation.

examples.title: Convert before storing fractional corrections
paragraphs: astype creates a converted array by default. np.iinfo reports the range of an integer type; it does not change that type's limits.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

integer_report = np.array([12,18,24], dtype=int)
integer_report[0] = 12.5
float_report = np.array([12,18,24], dtype=float)
float_report[0] = 12.5
print(integer_report.tolist())
print(float_report.tolist())
print(np.array([12,18]).astype(float).tolist())
print(np.iinfo(np.int8).max)
interpretation: The integer assignment lost the half-degree reading. Choose floating-point storage before the correction. An eight-bit signed integer cannot represent a count above the printed limit.

parts.title: 2. Distinguish Absence From a Measured Zero
paragraphs: NaN means not a number. It can mark an absent numerical observation or result from invalid arithmetic. Infinity can result from an unbounded or invalid numerical calculation. Neither is an ordinary finite thermometer reading.

NaN does not compare equal to itself. Use isnan to identify it and isfinite to require an ordinary finite value. Replacing these values is a modelling decision, so detecting them must come before silently filling them.

examples.title: Inspect the invalid positions explicitly
paragraphs: We keep a real zero beside a missing marker and an infinity. nanmean ignores NaNs, but it does not generally ignore infinities; we use a separate finite mask when that is the intended selection.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

report = np.array([0., np.nan, 18., np.inf])
print(np.isnan(report).tolist())
print(np.isfinite(report).tolist())
print(report[np.isfinite(report)].tolist())
print(np.nanmean(np.array([0., np.nan, 18.])))
examples.output:
[False, True, False, False]
[True, False, True, False]
[0.0, 18.0]
9.0
interpretation: The measured zero stays in the selected report. Ignoring missing entries changes which observations contribute; it does not prove the remaining observations represent the missing ones. An all-missing mean is still undefined.

parts.title: 3. Choose an Absolute and a Relative Tolerance
paragraphs: An absolute tolerance permits a fixed error in the result's units. A relative tolerance permits an error proportional to the reference value. np.isclose compares the difference with their combined allowance, using the second argument as the reference.

Use an explicit absolute tolerance near zero, and choose it for the required precision. allclose asks whether every aligned comparison passes. array_equal instead checks exact shape and value equality.

examples.title: Inspect rounding, then apply a stated tolerance
paragraphs: The first comparison exposes a familiar binary rounding difference. For the temperature checks we allow an absolute error of one thousandth of a degree and no relative allowance.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(np.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3, rtol=0, atol=1e-12))
actual = np.array([20.0001, 18.01])
expected = np.array([20., 18.])
print(np.isclose(actual, expected, rtol=0, atol=0.001).tolist())
print(np.allclose(actual, expected, rtol=0, atol=0.001))
interpretation: One temperature passes and the other does not. Increasing the tolerance until both pass would change the requirement instead of diagnosing the discrepancy.

parts.title: 4. Check the Shape Before Comparing Values
paragraphs: Approximate comparisons can broadcast compatible inputs. That is useful for some numerical checks but dangerous if a wrong result shape is supposed to fail. Confirm shape and finiteness first, then compare values.

Python's assert raises an AssertionError when a condition is false. It is useful in these learning checks and tests. For validation that must run in a deployed program, use an explicit condition and raise an error, because Python can disable assertions when run with optimisation.

examples.title: Make three independent expectations explicit
paragraphs: The wrong-shaped reference can broadcast and agree numerically, so agreement alone does not establish that our function returned the required vector. The assertions check the correctly shaped result separately.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

actual = np.array([20., 20.])
wrong_shape = np.array([[20.], [20.]])
print(np.allclose(actual, wrong_shape))
print(actual.shape == wrong_shape.shape)
expected = np.array([20., 20.])
assert actual.shape == expected.shape
assert np.isfinite(actual).all()
np.testing.assert_allclose(actual, expected, rtol=0, atol=0.001)
print("Shape, finite values, and tolerance checked.")
examples.output:
True
False
Shape, finite values, and tolerance checked.
interpretation: The testing helper raises an error when its numerical check fails and returns normally when it passes. A separate shape check makes our intended contract clear regardless of a comparison helper's broadcasting rules.
