title: Can We Repeat the Same Experiment?
blurb: Changing both a model and its sampled observations makes it difficult to explain a changed result. We need to keep track of the random choices so we can repeat a comparison.
openingTitle: Did Our New Method Help, or Did We Draw Easier Examples?
opening: Botie compares two ways of checking greenhouse sensors. If each method sees a different selection of readings, a changed score could come from the method or from the selection. We have changed two things at once.

A reproducible draw lets us hold the selection still while we investigate a change. It does not make that one selection representative of every possible draw. We need both repeatability and an honest account of variation.

history.title: Giving Simulated Experiments a Repeatable Starting Point
blocks: Numerical simulations need many values that behave like random draws, yet debugging also requires the ability to repeat an experiment. Pseudorandom generators address this by maintaining a state and updating it through a deterministic rule.

NumPy separates the bit generator from the interface that draws values. Its PCG64 documentation specifies how an initial seed establishes a stream. Our lesson uses this distinction to explain repeatability; the workshop receives already chosen indices and does not implement a random-number generator.

intuition.title: Name the observations before drawing
intuition.explanation: An index identifies a reading. Keeping the indices makes the selected observations inspectable.

intuition.title: Record a particular draw
intuition.explanation: A draw with replacement can ask for the same observation twice. Position one therefore appears twice here.

intuition.title: Follow the indices back to the data
intuition.explanation: The selected report contains the actual readings at those positions, including the repeated observation.

parts.title: 1. A Seed Starts a Sequence
paragraphs: We have stored readings in arrays and named readings in dictionaries. Generating random choices requires a different kind of object. A random generator contains a changing internal state and provides methods that use it to produce values. It is not itself the list of values it produces.

A seed gives us a repeatable way to initialise that state. Each draw advances it. Another call to the same generator continues the sequence; creating a new generator with the same setup starts a replay.
interpretation: We will create the generator in separate steps so that each piece has a clear purpose.

examples.title: Separate the seed, the generator, and the drawn array
paragraphs: Our seed is one integer. PCG64 is the algorithm that maintains the state and produces random bits. Generator supplies methods for turning those bits into the kinds of draws we request.

The integers method below requests three positions. Its lower limit is included and its upper limit is excluded. With four readings, the valid positions therefore run from zero through three. The size argument sets the number of requested entries.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

seed = 42
bit_generator = np.random.PCG64(seed)
rng = np.random.Generator(bit_generator)
positions = rng.integers(0, 4, size=3)

print(positions.tolist())
print(positions.shape)
interpretation: The result is an integer array containing three positions. The generator remains a separate object, ready for another request. This output is from the Python environment used by the site's challenges; record the library version and generator when preserving an experiment.

examples.title: A new draw and a replay are different requests
paragraphs: First we draw twice from one generator. Then we initialise another with the same algorithm and seed. Passing the PCG64 object directly into Generator combines the two construction steps from the previous example.
The array_equal function compares two arrays' shapes and entries and returns one Boolean result.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.Generator(np.random.PCG64(42))
first = rng.integers(0, 4, size=3)
second = rng.integers(0, 4, size=3)

replay_rng = np.random.Generator(np.random.PCG64(42))
replayed = replay_rng.integers(0, 4, size=3)

print(first.tolist())
print(second.tolist())
print(np.array_equal(first, replayed))
interpretation: The second request continued the first generator's sequence. The separate generator reproduced the first request. Consecutive draws can happen to contain the same values, so inequality is not the definition of a fresh draw. Advancing the generator's state is what makes it a new request.

parts.title: 2. Draw Positions, Then Retrieve Readings
paragraphs: Keeping the positions separates the choice of observations from the retrieval of their values. Once we have the positions, the lookup is completely determined. An integer index array can request the same position more than once, which is useful for sampling with replacement.
Sampling without replacement does not repeat a selected position. Bootstrapping deliberately allows repeats; splitting data into disjoint groups should not put the same observation in both groups.
interpretation: The repeated reading counts twice in this resample because its position was selected twice. It is not evidence that Botie independently measured that greenhouse twice.

examples.title: Retrieve values in the order the indices request them
paragraphs: The first array holds temperatures. The second holds integer positions into that array. Square brackets apply the recorded choices, including their order and repetitions. We round the displayed mean to four decimal places.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40], dtype=float)
indices = np.array([1, 1, 3])
selected = readings[indices]

print(indices.tolist())
print(selected.tolist())
print(np.round(selected.mean(), 4))
interpretation: The positions are whole numbers because they identify entries. The selected temperatures are floating-point values because that is what readings stores. We should not turn the index array into a set, since doing so would discard the repeated selection.

examples.title: Choose readings with or without replacement
paragraphs: default_rng is NumPy's convenient way to create a generator. It currently uses PCG64 by default; explicitly naming the bit generator, as earlier, also records that choice. choice draws from the values we supply. With replace=False, no input position can be chosen twice in one draw.
A size tuple asks for a table of draws. Here replacement is allowed for the second request, so a draw can include the same observation more than once.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

readings = np.array([10.,20.,30.,40.])
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
without_replacement = rng.choice(readings, size=3, replace=False)
print(without_replacement.size)
print(np.unique(without_replacement).size)
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
resamples = rng.choice(readings, size=(2,3), replace=True)
print(resamples.tolist())
print(np.round(resamples.mean(axis=1),4).tolist())
interpretation: The first input has distinct values, so its three unique selected values also demonstrate three distinct positions. In a dataset with equal-valued observations, different positions could still hold equal values. The two resamples happen to share a mean here, although their selected observations differ.

parts.title: 3. Keep a Fair Comparison Repeatable
paragraphs: If Botie compares two methods, both should see the same recorded draws before we attribute a changed result to the method. We can keep several draws in one two-dimensional index array: one row per draw, one position per selected observation.
Indexing a one-dimensional readings array with this index table produces a table of readings in the same arrangement. Each index is replaced by the value it selects.
interpretation: The two rows below are illustrative draws. The coding challenge will ask you to summarise a different pair.

examples.title: An index table becomes a table of selected readings
paragraphs: The integer table has two draws with three selections each. After retrieval, averaging along axis one combines the selections within each draw. It leaves one mean per draw.

title: Give a Reusable Calculation a Clear Contract
blurb: Copying a calculation into every exercise makes mistakes hard to repair. We will put the rule in a function, state what its inputs mean, and check it on more than one report.
openingTitle: Can We Explain the Rule Once and Use It Again?
opening: Botie keeps converting new greenhouse reports. If we copy the same calculation into each program, one copy may use a different offset or quietly change the original data. A named function gives the rule one place to live.
The name alone is not enough. The function needs a clear agreement about its inputs, output shape, units, and treatment of invalid data. We will build that agreement as part of the code.

history.title: Making Numerical Routines Reusable Without Losing Their Assumptions
blocks: Reusable numerical routines let programmers test one implementation and call it from many calculations. Their usefulness depends on the caller and the routine agreeing about dimensions, units, and valid inputs.

NumPy's array conversion and testing interfaces support those contracts. They let a Python function accept array-like input, validate its layout, and compare a result with a small independently checked example. The function remains responsible for its scientific assumptions.

intuition.title: Name the input meaning
intuition.explanation: The function receives Celsius readings in their original greenhouse order.

intuition.title: Keep the rule in one place

parts.title: 1. Separate a Function Definition From a Call
paragraphs: def introduces a function. Its parameters name the inputs inside the function; the indented body describes the work. Defining it does not yet perform the calculation. A call supplies actual arguments. return sends a result back to the caller.

Printing and returning are different: print displays something; return makes the result available to the next calculation. A function that only prints cannot be used as a numerical result in the same way.

examples.title: Define the conversion, then use its returned array
paragraphs: asarray accepts a list or array and requests floating-point values. The arithmetic creates the output without modifying the incoming readings.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

def to_fahrenheit(celsius):
    values = np.asarray(celsius, dtype=float)
    return values * 1.8 + 32

first = to_fahrenheit([12,18,24])
reference = to_fahrenheit([0,100])
print(np.round(first,1).tolist())
print(reference.tolist())
interpretation: The function has one local parameter, but two calls provide different data. Neither call needs a separate copy of the conversion rule.

parts.title: 2. Reject an Input That Does Not Match the Promise
paragraphs: Suppose the function promises one nonempty vector of finite readings. A matrix, an empty vector, or a NaN should produce a useful error. Check these conditions before performing the calculation.

A raise statement stops the function with an exception. ValueError is appropriate when an argument's value or arrangement is unsuitable. A caller can catch a particular exception with try and except when it has a meaningful response.

examples.title: Make the failed assumption visible
paragraphs: The three checks are separate because their error messages describe different problems. len is not a substitute for ndim: a matrix also has a length.
interpretation: The all reduction turns the finite mask into one Boolean, so Python's not is appropriate here. The error describes the input contract instead of letting a later shape failure obscure it.

parts.title: 3. Return the Reference Along With the Result
paragraphs: Some calculations first learn a reference, then apply it elsewhere. If Botie centres each new report on its own average, comparisons no longer share the same reference. Learn from the training readings once and pass that value to the next operation.
A function can return more than one result in a tuple. The caller can unpack that tuple into names that keep their meanings distinct.

examples.title: Keep the fitted reference separate from the new report
paragraphs: This example accepts already validated, nonempty finite vectors. The training average is learned before the new report is transformed.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

def centre_from_training(training, report):
    training = np.asarray(training, dtype=float)
    report = np.asarray(report, dtype=float)
    reference = training.mean()
    return reference, report - reference

reference, centred = centre_from_training([10,14], [12,18])
print(reference)
print(centred.tolist())
interpretation: The reference is one scalar and the centred report is an array. Returning both makes it possible to inspect the fitted value and reuse it without recalculating it from later observations.

parts.title: 4. Test More Than the First Demonstration
paragraphs: A check should describe what the function must do, not merely repeat the same implementation. Use reference cases with independently known answers, then include a changed input and a boundary case. Check shapes and whether the input was preserved.
A loop is useful here because we want to run a collection of separate test cases. It is not the numerical operation we are trying to vectorise.

examples.title: Check familiar reference temperatures and input preservation
paragraphs: A test case is a pair of input and expected-output lists. The loop unpacks each pair, calls the function, and checks its contract. The final report only prints if every assertion succeeds.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

def to_fahrenheit(celsius):
    return np.asarray(celsius, dtype=float) * 1.8 + 32

cases = [([0,100],[32,212]), ([-40],[-40])]
for values, expected in cases:
    original = np.array(values, dtype=float)
    saved = original.copy()
    result = to_fahrenheit(original)
    assert result.shape == original.shape
    np.testing.assert_allclose(result, expected, rtol=0, atol=1e-10)
    assert np.array_equal(original, saved)
print("2 cases passed; inputs preserved.")
interpretation: The tests do not fit a model or prove the conversion for every conceivable input. They check concrete expectations that would catch common mistakes in the rule and its handling of arrays.

title: Keep Enough of a Calculation to Run It Again
blurb: A printed table is not a complete experiment record. We will save arrays with their shapes and types, keep related arrays together, and check what survives when a report moves through a text file.
openingTitle: What Will Tomorrow's Program Need From Today's Work?
opening: Botie has prepared a feature table, fitted coefficients, and kept the greenhouse names. Tomorrow's program must load those pieces in the same order. Saving only a screenshot or a rounded list of predictions would not be enough to repeat the calculation.

NumPy can save one array in its native format, keep several arrays in a named archive, or exchange numbers as text. We will try each route and check both the values and the information needed to interpret them.

prerequisites.title: Give a Reusable Calculation a Clear Contract
Turn Several Measurements Into Several Predictions

history.title: Keeping Numerical Results Usable by the Next Program
blocks: Scientific programs need to exchange data and repeat earlier calculations. Plain text is inspectable, but it does not automatically preserve every array's type, shape, labels, or full numerical precision.

NumPy's NPY format records an array's dtype and shape with its values. NPZ archives collect named arrays, while text readers and writers serve simpler interchange needs. These formats preserve stored data, not the scientific meaning we forget to record.

intuition.title: Keep the model inputs
intuition.explanation: Observation rows must remain attached to their feature columns.

intuition.title: Keep the rule and the names
intuition.explanation: Coefficients and labels explain how the table is used.

intuition.title: Recompute after loading
intuition.explanation: A successful round trip restores the data and lets the same calculation run.

parts.title: 1. Save the Array, Not Only Its Printed Appearance
paragraphs: np.save writes one array in NPY format. np.load reads it back, including the dtype and shape. A printed string is intended for people; a saved numerical array is intended for another calculation.

These browser examples use BytesIO, a binary file held in memory. It follows the same read/write interface as a file without writing to your computer. Its contents are temporary and disappear when the Python runtime is reset. For a local Python program, a file path can be supplied instead.

examples.title: Write an array and read it back
paragraphs: BytesIO comes from Python's io module. Writing advances the file position, so seek(0) returns to the beginning before loading. We disallow pickle because these ordinary numerical arrays do not need Python-object deserialisation.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

from io import BytesIO

readings = np.array([[12.,18.],[14.,22.]], dtype=np.float64)
file = BytesIO()
np.save(file, readings, allow_pickle=False)
file.seek(0)
restored = np.load(file, allow_pickle=False)
print(restored.tolist())
print(restored.shape)
print(restored.dtype)
print(np.array_equal(restored, readings))
interpretation: The restored array has the same values, shape, and numerical representation. That does not tell it whether a column was temperature or humidity; metadata must supply those meanings.

parts.title: 2. Keep Related Arrays Under Explicit Names
paragraphs: An NPZ archive can hold several arrays. Keyword arguments to savez choose names by which they can be retrieved. This is useful when a feature table, a coefficient vector, and observation labels belong to the same calculation.

The archive is a resource that should be closed after reading. A with statement keeps it open for the indented block and closes it when the block ends. Keep any arrays needed later by assigning them within that block.

examples.title: Restore the pieces before recomputing the result
paragraphs: The labels are a regular NumPy string array, not arbitrary Python objects. Dictionary-like key lookup retrieves each named array from the archive.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

from io import BytesIO

X = np.array([[10.,40.],[20.,60.]])
weights = np.array([2.,0.1])
names = np.array(["north","south"])
file = BytesIO()
np.savez(file, features=X, weights=weights, names=names)
file.seek(0)
with np.load(file, allow_pickle=False) as saved:
    restored_X = saved["features"]
    restored_weights = saved["weights"]
    restored_names = saved["names"]
print(restored_names.tolist())
print((restored_X @ restored_weights).tolist())
interpretation: Names remain aligned with the rows. savez_compressed writes a compressed NPZ archive when reducing stored size is useful, with additional work for compression and decompression.

parts.title: 3. Read a Small Text Table Deliberately
paragraphs: Text is convenient for inspecting and sharing rows, but a reader must know the delimiter, which lines are headers, and what type to use. loadtxt is suitable for a regular numeric table with the stated format. genfromtxt provides additional handling for missing entries.
StringIO is the text counterpart to BytesIO. It lets this example read a tiny CSV entirely in memory. On disk, the reader can take a path instead.

examples.title: Keep the header separate from the numerical rows
paragraphs: Three quotes enclose a string spanning several lines. The delimiter says that commas separate fields. skiprows skips the one header line; it does not turn those names into automatic labels on the returned array.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

from io import StringIO

csv = StringIO("""temperature,humidity
12,50
18,60
""")
features = np.loadtxt(csv, delimiter=",", skiprows=1, ndmin=2)
print(features.tolist())
print(features.shape)
interpretation: The feature names still need to be stored separately. ndmin=2 keeps a table-shaped result even if a future report contains just one numerical row.

parts.title: 4. Record What a File Format Cannot Infer
paragraphs: A round-trip check should compare the loaded shape, dtype, values, and label ordering with the originals. Units, feature meanings, random settings, and library versions belong in the experiment record too. A saved array cannot reconstruct assumptions that were never recorded.

When writing text with savetxt, the format controls precision. A small number of decimal places may be fine for a human report, but it deliberately discards information needed for an exact numerical replay.

examples.title: Show the difference between a report and an exact record
paragraphs: We write two decimal places to a text file in memory, then reload it. allclose can accept the stated display error, while exact equality correctly reports that the original values were not fully preserved.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

from io import StringIO

original = np.array([[12.345,50.],[18.765,60.]])
text_file = StringIO()
np.savetxt(text_file, original, delimiter=",", fmt="%.2f")
text_file.seek(0)
restored = np.loadtxt(text_file, delimiter=",", ndmin=2)
print(restored.shape == original.shape)
print(np.array_equal(restored, original))
print(np.allclose(restored, original, rtol=0, atol=0.01))
interpretation: That loss of precision was a choice made by the writer. Use a native array file when exact preservation of the stored numerical entries is required.

title: When a Measurement Is Missing
blurb: An empty thermometer reading does not mean the greenhouse was at zero degrees. We need to distinguish what was measured from what we supplied to keep a calculation working.
openingTitle: What Should We Do With an Empty Cell?
opening: Botie opens the greenhouse report and finds a blank temperature. Perhaps the sensor lost power, or perhaps it stopped reporting when the greenhouse became too hot. Those possibilities have different implications.

A numerical method may still require a value in that position. We can supply a replacement, but we must keep clear that it is an estimate. Filling a cell makes an array usable; it does not recover the measurement that was never recorded.

history.title: The Missing Observation Has a Story Too
blocks: Incomplete records posed a problem for statistical inference long before modern neural networks. Ignoring an absent observation can change the group we describe, especially when absence is related to the value we wanted to measure.

Rubin's 1976 paper established conditions under which the missingness process can be ignored for particular forms of inference. It did not say that replacing every blank with an average is universally valid. Our invented greenhouse example uses mean replacement as a transparent baseline so we can inspect exactly what it assumes.

intuition.title: Leave the blank visible
intuition.explanation: A blank is an unknown temperature. Writing zero there would assert something we did not observe.

intuition.title: Use only the recorded training values
intuition.explanation: The two observed training readings give a replacement reference. A later observation must not help choose it.

intuition.title: Keep the new report's measured entries
intuition.explanation: Only the missing entry changes. The recorded temperature stays intact.

parts.title: 1. Separate Missing From Zero
paragraphs: Zero is a possible temperature. Missing means we do not know the temperature. These must remain different values. The workshop uses a blank cell represented internally by null; Python uses a floating-point missing marker called NaN.
First identify which entries were observed. Do not let the missing marker participate in an ordinary average.
interpretation: The set of observed readings may itself be biased. If the hottest sensors stop reporting, its average will not describe the missing temperatures well.

parts.title: 2. Learn the Replacement From Training Data
paragraphs: Mean imputation uses the average of observed training values as a replacement. Imputation means supplying missing entries. We estimate that reference once during fitting, then reuse it on later data.
parts.calculation:
Training reference = (10 + 14) / 2 = 12
New report:    [missing, 18]
Filled report: [12, 18]
interpretation: Including the new report's measured temperature when choosing the reference would change the fitted preprocessing after seeing new data. For evaluation, it would let held-out observations influence the preparation.

parts.title: 3. Keep Track of What Was Replaced
paragraphs: A missingness indicator records which values were supplied. A one in that indicator means the original entry was absent; a zero means it was measured. That information can matter if missingness is related to how the records were collected.
parts.calculation:
New report:          [missing, 18]
Missing indicator:   [1, 0]
Filled temperatures: [12, 18]
interpretation: The indicator preserves a distinction, not a guarantee. It cannot recover the absent reading. Mean replacement also understates variability if we later treat supplied values as independent observations.

parts.title: 4. Choose the Assumption Before the Convenience
paragraphs: A median can resist extreme observed values. A fixed replacement may have domain meaning. More elaborate methods use relationships among features, and some models handle missing entries directly. Each choice still needs evaluation under the intended conditions.

If every training value is missing, there is no observed mean to calculate. Stop and choose a documented fallback or remove that feature for a reason. Silently inventing a zero would hide the failure.
interpretation: Botie's construction must learn from the training readings and fill the new report. It must preserve every value that was actually observed.

quiz.prompt: A missing thermometer reading means the temperature was zero.
quiz.because: Absence is not a physical temperature. Zero would be an invented measurement.

quiz.prompt: Which observations establish our replacement?
quiz.because: The replacement is a fitted preprocessing parameter. It is learned from the observed training values and reused.

quiz.prompt: Keeping a missingness indicator can distinguish supplied values from measured values.
quiz.because: The indicator preserves which entries were absent, although it does not recover their true temperatures.

practice.title: Can you fill the report without using it to learn the replacement?
practice.question: Can you fill the report without using it to learn the replacement?
task: Use only observed training values to calculate the replacement mean. Fill missing values in the new report.
Print the mean with one decimal place, then the completed report as a list.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
training = np.array([10., np.nan, 14.])
report = np.array([np.nan, 18.])
# Learn from training, then fill report.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
training = np.array([10., np.nan, 14.])
report = np.array([np.nan, 18.])
reference = training[~np.isnan(training)].mean()
filled = np.where(np.isnan(report), reference, report)
print(f'{reference:.1f}')
print(filled.tolist())
hints: np.isnan identifies the missing markers. Invert that mask to keep observed training values.
np.where can choose the replacement only where the report's missing mask is true.

practice.title: Can a later reader tell which temperatures were measured?
practice.question: Can a later reader tell which temperatures were measured?
task: Learn a mean from the new training array. Print the filled report, then a list of integer missingness indicators.
Record the indicator before replacing values.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
training = np.array([6.,12.,np.nan,18.])
report = np.array([9.,np.nan,15.,np.nan])
# Preserve missingness before filling.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
training = np.array([6.,12.,np.nan,18.])
report = np.array([9.,np.nan,15.,np.nan])
missing = np.isnan(report)
reference = training[~np.isnan(training)].mean()
print(np.where(missing,reference,report).tolist())
print(missing.astype(int).tolist())
hints: Keep the missing mask in a variable before filling.
Converting a Boolean mask to int turns false and true into zero and one.

build.title: Fill a greenhouse report from its training reference
build.problem: Botie's report has absent temperatures. Learn a replacement from observed training readings, then fill only the missing report entries.
build.challenge: Select the observed training values, find their mean, and use that mean to replace blanks in the new report.
build.why: The training branch supplies one reference. The report branch retains its measurements and uses that reference only at absent entries.
build.limitation: Mean replacement is a baseline. It cannot recover the true missing values or represent uncertainty about them.

title: Categories Without an Invented Ranking
blurb: A roof can be glass, plastic, or mesh. Assigning those names arbitrary numbers can accidentally suggest a ranking. We need a representation that preserves category membership without inventing a numerical relationship.
openingTitle: Is Glass Really Twice as Much Roof as Plastic?
opening: Botie wants to include greenhouse roof material in a temperature model. The materials are glass, plastic, and mesh. A model needs usable inputs, so assigning each name an ID seems like a reasonable start.

But an ID is an address, not a measurement. If a numerical model multiplies those IDs by a shared coefficient, it treats the gaps between IDs as meaningful. We need a way to indicate the material without claiming that one material is twice another.

history.title: Giving Each Category Its Own Question
blocks: Statistical models need representations for properties that are names rather than quantities. Indicator variables answer separate membership questions, allowing categories to contribute without forcing their arbitrary codes onto a numerical scale.

Modern preprocessing libraries document one-hot encoding as one way to create those indicators. Our roof materials are an invented example. The practical contribution we need is the representation: one fixed column per known category, with a clear policy for unfamiliar categories.

intuition.title: Start with names
intuition.explanation: The roof materials identify categories. Their order here is simply our chosen vocabulary order.

intuition.title: Ask one question per material
intuition.explanation: Each row says whether that roof matches each vocabulary entry.

intuition.title: Reuse the same column meanings
intuition.explanation: Another glass roof must receive the same representation. Changing column order changes what a fitted coefficient means.

parts.title: 1. Distinguish an ID From a Quantity
paragraphs: A temperature difference has units and a physical interpretation. A material ID does not. Renaming glass from ID one to ID seven should not change the properties of the roof.

Some model families handle categorical IDs specially. A plain numerical coefficient does not: it will multiply the number it receives. We therefore need to consider how the model interprets the representation.
interpretation: Do not conclude that every integer-coded feature is invalid. An ordered category or a categorical-aware algorithm has different assumptions. Our problem concerns unordered names passed to ordinary numerical operations.

parts.title: 2. Make a Column for Each Membership Question
paragraphs: Choose a vocabulary, then compare each material with every entry. A matching column receives one and the other columns receive zero. This is called one-hot encoding when exactly one column is active.
parts.calculation:
Column order: glass, plastic, mesh
glass → [1, 0, 0]
mesh  → [0, 0, 1]
interpretation: The zeros do not say that a roof has no properties. They say that it is not a member of those particular categories.

parts.title: 3. Keep the Vocabulary Fixed After Fitting
paragraphs: The model's coefficients attach to column positions. If we fit with glass first and later move mesh into the first position, the arithmetic still runs while the meaning changes. Fit the vocabulary on training data and preserve its order.

An unfamiliar material needs an explicit policy. We can reserve an unknown category, reject the record for review, or use an all-zero representation with care. This workshop uses all zeros and makes that policy visible.
parts.calculation:
Vocabulary: [glass, plastic, mesh]
Unknown foil roof → [0, 0, 0]
interpretation: All zeros cannot identify which unfamiliar material appeared. If one known category is also represented by all zeros after dropping a reference column, unknowns become ambiguous unless handled separately.

parts.title: 4. Decide What the Representation Leaves Out
paragraphs: Separate indicators let a model learn separate contributions. They do not teach it that two materials have similar insulation or cost. If those measured properties matter, we may want additional features that describe them directly.

With an intercept in a linear model, all category columns together create a redundant description. Dropping a reference column is one way to remove that redundancy. We keep all columns here so the membership mechanism is easy to inspect.
interpretation: Botie's workshop constructs the indicator table. Later modelling lessons decide how to fit coefficients to it.

quiz.prompt: Why are arbitrary material IDs risky for a plain numerical coefficient?
options: The IDs may imply meaningful numerical gaps
Numbers cannot represent text in any form
quiz.because: A numerical coefficient uses the size of the ID. Our arbitrary category numbering does not justify that relationship.

quiz.prompt: One-hot column order can change freely after fitting.
quiz.because: Fitted coefficients refer to the original column meanings.

quiz.prompt: What does our all-zero row for foil tell us?
options: Foil was the first training category
Foil did not match the supplied vocabulary
quiz.because: The comparison found no matching known material. It makes no physical claim about foil.

practice.title: Can you give each roof the right membership row?
practice.question: Can you give each roof the right membership row?

Print the integer indicator table as a nested list. Unrecognised materials must receive all zeros.

materials = np.array(['glass','mesh','glass','foil'])

encoded = (materials[:,None] == vocabulary).astype(int)

hints: Give materials a column axis so each row can be compared with all vocabulary entries.
An equality comparison gives Booleans; convert them to integer indicators.

practice.title: Which rows need an unknown-material review?
practice.question: Which rows need an unknown-material review?
task: Build the same encoding for plastic, foil, and mesh. A row with no active indicator needs review.
Print the encoded table and then a Boolean list of rows needing review.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
vocabulary = np.array(['glass','plastic','mesh'])
materials = np.array(['plastic','foil','mesh'])
# Encode, then inspect each row's total.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
vocabulary = np.array(['glass','plastic','mesh'])
materials = np.array(['plastic','foil','mesh'])
encoded = (materials[:,None] == vocabulary).astype(int)
print(encoded.tolist())
print((encoded.sum(axis=1) == 0).tolist())
hints: Sum within each row, preserving one total per roof.
A zero row total means no vocabulary category matched.

build.title: Represent the greenhouse roof materials
build.problem: Botie needs a stable numerical description of roof material without treating an arbitrary ID as a quantity. We will build the three indicator columns separately, then arrange them into rows.
build.challenge: Read each of the three vocabulary entries by its zero-based index. Compare all materials with each entry to make a column of indicators. Collect the first two columns, append the third column, then swap rows and columns so each material has one row. Unknown materials receive all zeros.

sources.vocabulary: Three training categories in fixed order

build.why: Each comparison builds a separate category column. Collecting and transposing those columns puts one material's answers together in each row.
build.limitation: This construction uses exactly three vocabulary categories so the comparisons remain visible. It does not fit a model or remove redundant columns.

title: When the End Is Beside the Beginning
blurb: The hour after 23 is zero, yet ordinary subtraction puts those hour numbers far apart. A repeating feature needs a representation that keeps its beginning beside its end.
openingTitle: Why Does Midnight Look So Far From Eleven?
opening: Botie records greenhouse temperatures throughout the day. If we encode the hour as a number from zero to 23, late evening and early morning sit at opposite ends of the number line. On a clock they are neighbours.

The issue is the shape of the information. An hour of the day repeats after a full turn. We can preserve that relationship by placing each hour around a circle and describing its position with two coordinates.

history.title: Representing a Repeating Cycle as a Position
blocks: Time-related measurements create a practical modelling problem: day, week, and seasonal cycles have boundaries in their written numbering that are not boundaries in the phenomenon. A representation that ignores repetition can make neighbouring times look unrelated.

Sine and cosine coordinates use the familiar geometry of a circle to preserve a cycle's continuity. Scikit-learn's time-feature example documents this representation among several modelling choices. Our greenhouse clock is an invented teaching example, and we are not presenting the circle representation as a newly invented algorithm.

intuition.title: The written hour wraps around
intuition.explanation: The order continues through midnight. Zero belongs immediately after 23 on the next day.

intuition.title: Use two coordinates on a clock face
intuition.explanation: Quarter turns give easily recognised positions. The coordinate order here is cosine, then sine.

scene.caption: Invented clock positions on a unit circle. One full day returns to the starting point.

intuition.title: The cycle closes
intuition.explanation: The position at hour 24 is the same as the position at hour zero. Here eleven at night and one in the morning sit beside midnight. The date must be stored separately if it matters.

scene.caption: Invented clock positions on a unit circle. One full day returns to the starting point.

parts.title: 1. Decide What Repeats
paragraphs: An hour of day repeats every 24 hours. Elapsed time since an experiment began does not. We should use a circular representation only for the repeating feature, while keeping nonrepeating information elsewhere.
For this lesson, the input is an hour measured from midnight and the period is 24 hours. Fractions such as half past six can be represented too.
interpretation: The period is a modelling assumption. A weekly pattern needs a different period, and calendar months do not all contain the same number of days.

parts.title: 2. Turn the Fraction of a Cycle Into an Angle
paragraphs: Divide the hour by the period to find how far around the cycle we are. A full circle is two pi radians. Multiplying by that full-turn angle places the hour around the circle.
parts.calculation:
Hour 6:  fraction = 6 / 24 = 1/4
         angle = (1/4) × 2π = π/2
Hour 12: fraction = 12 / 24 = 1/2
         angle = (1/2) × 2π = π
interpretation: Radians are a way to measure an angle. The important fact here is that a full period brings us back to the same position.

parts.title: 3. Use Both Coordinates
paragraphs: Cosine gives the horizontal coordinate of our point on a unit circle. Sine gives its vertical coordinate. We need both because a single coordinate is shared by different positions.
interpretation: Sine alone would give zero at both midnight and noon. The cosine coordinate distinguishes them. Near midnight, both coordinates change smoothly across the written day boundary.

parts.title: 4. The Representation Is Not the Whole Prediction Rule
paragraphs: Two coordinates tell a model where we are in the cycle. They do not guarantee that the daily temperature follows a simple sinusoid. Weather, heating controls, and the season can still matter.

A linear combination of this single sine-cosine pair describes one smooth daily oscillation. More complicated recurring shapes may need additional harmonics, splines, or a flexible model. Choose that complexity through appropriate evaluation.
interpretation: The workshop builds the pair for one hour. The Python practice builds it for several times and then changes the period to a week.

quiz.prompt: Hour 24 and hour zero share the same cyclical position.
quiz.because: They are separated by one full period. A separate date feature would be needed to distinguish the days.

quiz.prompt: Why do we keep both sine and cosine?
options: To distinguish positions that share one coordinate
To create an arbitrary category ID
quiz.because: For example, sine alone gives zero at both midnight and noon.

quiz.prompt: Encoding the hour on a circle proves temperature follows a single smooth daily wave.
quiz.because: The representation preserves periodic position. It does not establish the complete relationship between hour and temperature.

practice.title: Where do the quarter-day readings sit on the circle?
practice.question: Where do the quarter-day readings sit on the circle?
task: For hours 0, 6, 12, and 18, create rows containing cosine first and sine second.
Print the nested list rounded to four decimal places.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
hours = np.array([0.,6.,12.,18.])
# Convert to angles, then make two-coordinate rows.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
hours = np.array([0.,6.,12.,18.])
angles = hours / 24 * (2*np.pi)
print(np.round(np.column_stack((np.cos(angles),np.sin(angles))),4).tolist())
hints: One full day maps to two pi radians.
np.column_stack keeps the two coordinate columns in the stated order.

practice.title: Can the same construction describe the week?
practice.question: Can the same construction describe the week?
task: Use day positions 0, 1, and 6 in a seven-day cycle. Day zero is our chosen start of the week.
Print cosine-sine rows rounded to four decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
days = np.array([0.,1.,6.])
# Use the weekly period.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
days = np.array([0.,1.,6.])
angles = days / 7 * (2*np.pi)
print(np.round(np.column_stack((np.cos(angles),np.sin(angles))),4).tolist())
hints: Only the period changes: use seven rather than 24.
Day six and day zero are neighbours around the weekly cycle.

build.title: Give the greenhouse clock two coordinates
build.problem: Botie's hour feature should preserve that the day repeats. We will return the position around a circle, with cosine first and sine second.
build.challenge: Divide the hour by the period, multiply by a full turn of 2π radians, then collect cosine and sine in that order. The Full turn source supplies 2π.
build.why: Dividing identifies the fraction of a cycle. Sine and cosine locate that fraction on a circle, so a full turn returns to the start.
build.limitation: This encodes a fixed-period feature. It does not fit a temperature curve or handle calendar irregularities.

title: What Does One Row Represent?
blurb: Two identical-looking rows might be a duplicated import or two genuine observations. We need to establish a record's identity before cleaning a dataset or trusting its counts.
openingTitle: Did We Observe It Twice, or Import It Twice?
opening: Botie joins two greenhouse log files and finds the same event ID twice. If both entries describe the same measurement, counting both gives that event extra influence. If two different events happen to have the same temperature, removing one would discard real information.
The distinction comes from what a row represents. We need an event identity, a time, a unit, and a collection rule before deciding which repetitions are errors.

history.title: Why a Dataset Needs Its Own Instructions

sources.title: Gebru and colleagues: Datasheets for Datasets

blocks: A dataset can outlive the people who remember how it was collected. When collection details disappear, later users may mistake a convenient table for a complete description of a population.

Gebru and colleagues introduced datasheets for datasets in 2018, with a later journal publication, to document matters such as motivation, composition, collection, and recommended uses. Our duplicate-log exercise handles one small part of that broader problem: recording what an observation means before deciding how to clean it.

intuition.title: Two exports can overlap
intuition.explanation: The same event identifier appears in both files. It names one event even though the import contains two rows.

intuition.title: Count the distinct event identities
intuition.explanation: There are three distinct IDs. We have not yet decided which conflicting version to keep if repeated IDs disagree.

intuition.title: Count the excess copies
intuition.explanation: One imported row exceeds the distinct event count. This is a duplication audit, not an automatic cleaning decision.

parts.title: 1. Define the Unit of Observation
paragraphs: A row might represent one greenhouse, one thermometer reading, or one daily summary. These are different units of observation. If we combine them without checking, the row count stops having a clear meaning.
For this example, one row represents one sensor event, and each event is assigned a stable ID. Repeated IDs therefore deserve inspection. Repeated temperature values alone do not.
interpretation: A primary key is a field, or combination of fields, intended to identify one record. It is useful only when the collection process actually respects that meaning.

parts.title: 2. Audit Repeated Identities
paragraphs: Count all imported rows, then count distinct event IDs. Their difference reports excess copies. An ID appearing three times contributes two excess copies, not three.
parts.calculation:
Imported IDs: [101, 102, 102, 103]
Total rows = 4
Distinct event IDs = 3
Excess copies = 4 - 3 = 1
interpretation: This count tells us how much duplication to investigate. It does not tell us whether two versions contain identical measurements or which one is authoritative.

parts.title: 3. Check Values Against Their Meaning
paragraphs: After identity, check units, timestamp conventions, required fields, and plausible ranges. A measurement in Fahrenheit can look like an unusually warm Celsius reading while remaining a perfectly valid number.

Keep a reason for every exclusion or correction. A surprising value may be a faulty sensor, but it may also be the event we are trying to detect. Deleting surprises because they complicate the model can remove the signal.
interpretation: Quality checks should separate impossible records, inconsistent records, and unusual but possible observations. They do not all deserve the same response.

parts.title: 4. Preserve the Evidence Behind a Cleaned Table
paragraphs: Retain the original records and document the transformation into the modelling table. If duplicate IDs disagree, resolve the conflict using the source system's rules rather than whichever row happens to arrive first.

The workshop only measures excess copies. A real cleaning workflow also needs a conflict policy and an audit trail. Later validation must keep copies or related observations together so they cannot appear on both sides of an evaluation split.
interpretation: In the coding exercise, distinct-ID counting is enough because the requested result is an audit count, not a cleaned temperature estimate.

quiz.prompt: Which repetition identifies a potential duplicate event in our example?
options: Two events at the same temperature
Two rows with the same event ID
Two readings from the same greenhouse on different days
quiz.because: The stable event ID is defined to identify a single observation.

quiz.prompt: An event ID appearing three times contributes two excess copies.
quiz.because: One copy represents the distinct event; the other two exceed that count.

quiz.prompt: A duplicate count tells us which conflicting temperature is correct.
quiz.because: Counting identities does not resolve disagreements between versions.

build.title: Audit repeated greenhouse events
build.problem: Botie combined sensor exports that may overlap. Each stable ID names one event, so extra copies should be counted before analysis.
build.challenge: Return the number of imported rows beyond the number of distinct event IDs.
build.why: The two branches count all records and distinct identities. Subtracting them measures extra copies rather than genuine repeated values.
build.limitation: This audit assumes IDs identify events reliably. It does not decide which conflicting record should be kept.

title: What Could We Know at Prediction Time?
topic: Keep Future Answers Out of Training
blurb: A model can appear remarkably accurate when a feature contains information that arrives after the decision. We need to reconstruct what was actually available when each prediction would have been made.
openingTitle: Can We Predict a Repair Using the Completed Repair Report?
opening: Botie wants to predict at noon whether a greenhouse sensor will need repair later that day. The data export includes a morning reading, a noon reading, and a completed repair report entered that evening.
The evening report could make the prediction look easy. It may even state the answer. But it was not available at noon, so using it would test a different task from the one we intended to solve.

history.title: When a Successful Evaluation Used Unavailable Information

sources.title: Kaufman and colleagues: Leakage in Data Mining (2012)
Scikit-learn: Common pitfalls and data leakage

blocks: As data-mining systems combined many records and preprocessing steps, evaluation could accidentally give a model information unavailable in the real prediction setting. High scores then measured access to privileged evidence as well as predictive ability.

Kaufman and colleagues examined leakage as information about a target that is not legitimately available to the prediction process. Our invented repair records make the timing issue explicit. Other forms include fitting preprocessing on test data or placing copies of an observation on both sides of a split.

intuition.title: Fix the decision time
intuition.explanation: The task is to make the decision at noon. That time determines the boundary of available evidence.

intuition.title: Check when each field became available
intuition.explanation: Use availability time, not merely the date written inside a later report.

intuition.title: Keep only the evidence available then
intuition.explanation: The boundary includes the noon reading under this exercise's convention. The evening report is excluded.

parts.title: 1. Define the Decision Before Selecting Features
paragraphs: State what is predicted, for whom, and at what time. Without that definition, we cannot judge whether a feature was available legitimately.
Our task is a noon prediction of later repair need. A completed evening report fails the timing requirement even if it is stored in the same row as the morning measurements.
interpretation: A column's name is not enough. Investigate how the value was created, updated, and joined into the table.

parts.title: 2. Compare Availability With the Cutoff
paragraphs: Each field has an availability time. Keep it only when that time is at or before the prediction cutoff. The workshop uses whole hours to make this boundary visible.
parts.calculation:
Prediction cutoff: 12
Availability times: [9, 12, 18]
Available by cutoff: [1, 1, 0]
interpretation: The timestamp of the underlying event can differ from the time the system learned about it. A report describing a morning event but uploaded in the evening still cannot be used at noon.

parts.title: 3. Keep Fitting Inside the Evaluation Boundary
paragraphs: Leakage does not require an obviously future-looking column. A mean, vocabulary, selected feature, or imputation reference learned using held-out observations has also crossed the evaluation boundary.

Split first according to the intended prediction setting. Fit preprocessing and the model on training data. Apply those fitted choices to validation or test data without relearning from the held-out group.
interpretation: Pipelines help with the order of fitting operations. They cannot determine whether a raw field was available at the intended decision time. That requires knowledge of the data collection process.

parts.title: 4. Test the Procedure You Can Actually Run
paragraphs: A realistic evaluation replays the information constraints of deployment. Time order, delayed labels, related entities, and record updates may all matter. A random row split is not automatically wrong, but it answers the wrong question when it ignores the dependency we care about.
The workshop returns the eligible measurements in their original order. It does not decide whether those features are useful or ethically appropriate; it checks the stated timing boundary.
interpretation: Removing leakage may lower the score. That is a better measurement of the intended task, not a reason to put the unavailable information back.

quiz.prompt: A report entered at 18:00 was available for a 12:00 prediction just because it describes a morning event.
quiz.because: Availability depends on when the prediction system could access it, not only when the described event happened.

quiz.prompt: Where should a replacement mean be learned during evaluation?
options: From the full dataset before splitting
quiz.because: Preprocessing parameters are fitted choices and must respect the same boundary as the model.

quiz.prompt: A pipeline can determine whether a raw field was uploaded after the decision.
quiz.because: A pipeline controls fitting steps. The feature's real availability still needs to be established from its provenance.

title: When the Important Class Is Rare
topic: Keep Future Answers Out of Training
blurb: If almost every sensor is healthy, predicting healthy every time can look accurate while missing every failure. We need to inspect what the score says about each class.
openingTitle: How Did a Model Miss Every Failure and Still Look Good?
opening: Botie checks a batch containing 95 healthy sensors and five failed sensors. A rule that always says healthy gets most answers right. It also fails at the entire reason we might have built an alert system.
The class counts shape both the learning problem and the score. We need to keep the rare class visible, then decide how different mistakes should influence training and decisions.

history.title: Learning From a Class That Appears Only Occasionally
blocks: Classification datasets often contain many examples of one outcome and few of another. Researchers found that a method could favour the majority while performing poorly on the minority that mattered to the application.

Chawla and colleagues' 2002 SMOTE paper studied synthetic minority oversampling, creating additional minority examples between nearby observations. That is one response to imbalance, not a universal remedy. Our lesson first makes the evaluation problem visible; it does not generate synthetic sensor records.

intuition.title: Count both classes
intuition.explanation: The data contain many more healthy sensors than failed ones.

intuition.title: Inspect the always-healthy rule
intuition.explanation: The rule gets all healthy sensors right and misses all failures.

intuition.title: Give each class a visible score
intuition.explanation: The class-specific recalls reveal the failure that overall accuracy conceals.

parts.title: 1. Count the Mistakes the Task Cares About
paragraphs: Accuracy divides all correct predictions by all examples. If one class dominates the dataset, it also dominates that average. The problem is not that the arithmetic is wrong; the score answers a question that may be insufficient for our task.
interpretation: A high overall score does not establish that rare events are being found. Start by inspecting the class counts and the confusion matrix.

parts.title: 2. Give Each Class an Equal Place in the Summary
paragraphs: Recall asks what fraction of a class was correctly identified. Balanced accuracy averages those recalls, giving each class equal weight in the summary regardless of its count.
For the always-healthy rule, the healthy recall is perfect and the failure recall is zero.
interpretation: This makes the neglected class visible. It still does not specify the cost of a false alarm or a missed failure, and it does not replace the individual class scores.

parts.title: 3. Separate Training Choices From Evaluation Choices
paragraphs: We can weight training losses, resample training examples, or change the decision threshold. These are different interventions. Loss weighting changes the fitting objective; resampling changes the examples presented; a threshold changes how scores become actions.
Fit these choices using training and validation data. Oversampling before splitting can place related or duplicated information into both training and evaluation sets.
interpretation: A balanced training sample does not imply balanced deployment data. Keep the final evaluation distribution appropriate to the real task, and report the class counts used.

parts.title: 4. More Copies Are Not More Independent Evidence
paragraphs: Repeating a rare observation can make it influence training more, but it does not create a new independent observation. Synthetic examples introduce additional assumptions about which points are plausible.

For a rare class, score estimates can also be unstable because they depend on few cases. Report that limitation and inspect which mistakes occurred. The workshop constructs balanced accuracy from separate correct and total counts for both classes.
interpretation: An evaluation set with no examples of a required class cannot estimate that class's recall. Do not quietly replace an undefined recall with a reassuring value.

quiz.prompt: What did the always-healthy rule achieve on failures?
quiz.because: It predicted healthy for all five failed sensors, so it detected none.

quiz.prompt: Balanced accuracy gives equal weight to the two class recalls here.
quiz.because: It averages the class-specific recalls rather than weighting them by their class counts.

quiz.prompt: Duplicating a rare observation creates independent evidence about another sensor.
quiz.because: It changes the observation's influence, not how many independent observations were collected.

title: What Must a Model Improve On?
blurb: A complicated predictor needs a simple comparison. Before fitting one, we can measure how well a rule that always predicts a training average performs on new observations.
openingTitle: Would the Average Have Done Just as Well?
opening: Botie has a new model for greenhouse temperature. Its error sounds small, but small compared with what? If a simple rule would do just as well, the extra complexity has not yet earned its place.

We will start with a deliberately limited predictor: use the average training temperature for every new observation. That gives us a baseline, a result the more elaborate method should improve under the same evaluation conditions.

history.title: A Prediction Needs a Reference for Comparison
blocks: Predictive modelling needs control comparisons. Without them, a score cannot show whether a method gained anything from its inputs beyond a simple summary of previous outcomes.

Modern evaluation libraries preserve this practice through baseline estimators that ignore input features and predict a training summary. This is not an invention claim for one library. Our invented greenhouse example uses the training mean to make the comparison explicit before introducing more capable predictors.

intuition.title: Learn a single training reference
intuition.explanation: The baseline sees the training outcomes and no features. Its only fitted value is their mean.

intuition.title: Predict before inspecting the answers
intuition.explanation: Every held-out observation receives that same reference. The held-out answers do not change it.

intuition.title: Measure the errors
intuition.explanation: The baseline overpredicts one observation and underpredicts the other. Squaring keeps their sizes from cancelling.

parts.title: 1. Choose a Baseline That Matches the Task
paragraphs: A regression baseline might predict a mean or median. A classification baseline might use the majority class. A forecast might repeat the latest observation or the matching season. The baseline should be simple but relevant.
For our temperature example we will use the mean, because we will score squared errors. Among constant predictions, the training mean minimises the sum of squared training errors.
interpretation: This fitted constant ignores inputs such as sunlight and heating settings. It establishes what we can achieve before using those features.

parts.title: 2. Freeze the Rule Before Evaluating It
paragraphs: Apply the fitted constant to held-out observations. Do not replace it with the held-out mean. That would use information the predictor did not have when making those predictions.
interpretation: A baseline must obey the same information boundary as the model it is compared with.

parts.title: 3. Score Both Methods on the Same Observations
paragraphs: Mean squared error averages the squared differences between predictions and answers. We need the same units, same held-out examples, and same metric for a fair comparison.
interpretation: A model with lower error on different examples has not yet won this comparison. Shared evaluation examples let us compare their mistakes directly.

parts.title: 4. Ask What an Improvement Actually Buys
paragraphs: A small reduction in average error may not justify greater latency, maintenance, or instability. Inspect which observations improve and which get worse. Repeat the evaluation when the dataset is small or the fitting procedure is variable.

The baseline is a reference, not a target that guarantees usefulness once beaten. A temperature predictor may still be unsuitable for a particular control decision even after improving its average score.
interpretation: The workshop builds the whole baseline evaluation from training outcomes and held-out answers. It must not learn its constant from the test branch.

quiz.prompt: Which data determine the baseline's constant?
quiz.because: The training mean is fitted before we evaluate new observations.

quiz.prompt: Both methods should be scored on the same held-out observations.
quiz.because: Otherwise the difficulty of the evaluation data is another changing factor.

quiz.prompt: Beating a baseline guarantees the model is suitable for deployment.
quiz.because: Usefulness also depends on the size and nature of the improvement, uncertainty, and application requirements.

title: Would More Examples Help?
blurb: Before collecting more data or choosing a more flexible model, we can examine how training and validation errors change as the training set grows.
openingTitle: Should We Collect More Readings or Change the Rule?
opening: Botie's temperature model makes errors on new days. We could collect more days, or choose a more flexible rule. Those changes address different problems, so it helps to inspect the behaviour we already have.

Fit the same kind of model using several training-set sizes and measure both training and validation error. The resulting learning curves show how the method responds to more examples. They provide evidence for a decision, not a promise about what the next batch will do.

prerequisites.title: What Must a Model Improve On?

history.title: Model Comparisons Depend on How Much Data We Have

sources.title: Perlich, Provost, and Simonoff: A Learning-Curve Analysis (2003)

blocks: A comparison at one dataset size can hide how two learning methods respond as more examples become available. A method that works well with few observations need not remain the best choice with many.

Perlich, Provost, and Simonoff's 2003 study compared tree induction and logistic regression through learning curves. Our supplied greenhouse errors are invented illustrations, not results from that study or a model trained in this widget. They let us inspect the interpretation before running larger fitting experiments.

intuition.title: Fit with different numbers of examples
intuition.explanation: Each column refers to the same model family fitted with a different amount of training data.

intuition.title: Keep the two errors separate
intuition.explanation: Training error measures the fitted examples. Validation error measures examples excluded from fitting. These illustrative curves show the two quantities coming closer as the training set grows.

scene.caption: Invented errors for illustration. The lower green line is training MSE; the upper red line is validation MSE. No model was fitted to produce these teaching values.

intuition.title: Watch the gap alongside the actual errors
intuition.explanation: The gap narrows here as more data arrive. A narrow gap alone would not be enough if both errors remained large.

parts.title: 1. Change the Training Size, Not Everything at Once
paragraphs: Choose several training sizes. At each size, fit the same procedure from scratch, including preprocessing. Evaluate the fitted model on its training subset and on data excluded from that fit.
Keep the metric and validation design consistent. Repeat subsets or splits when possible so an unusually easy selection does not masquerade as a trend.
interpretation: A learning curve varies the amount of training data. A validation curve instead varies a model setting. The axes answer different questions.

parts.title: 2. Inspect Both Curves Before Summarising Them
paragraphs: Low training error with much larger validation error suggests the fitted rule depends heavily on details of the training sample. If the gap shrinks as data increase, collecting more comparable data may help.
If both errors stay high and close together, the current representation or model may be too limited, although noise, poor measurements, or distribution mismatch can produce similar symptoms.
parts.calculation:
At 10 examples: gap = 9 - 1 = 8
At 50 examples: gap = 6 - 2 = 4
At 100 examples: gap = 4 - 3 = 1
interpretation: The supplied illustration shows a narrowing gap and improving validation error. It is not a universal shape that all models must follow.

parts.title: 3. Do Not Mistake a Small Gap for a Good Predictor
paragraphs: Subtracting the two errors measures their difference, not their absolute quality. Equal errors can both be unacceptable. Compare the validation score with the baseline and with the needs of the application.
interpretation: This gap is smaller than in the earlier illustration, yet the validation error is much worse. A single gap score cannot replace the two curves.

parts.title: 4. Use the Pattern to Choose the Next Experiment
paragraphs: A curve can suggest whether to investigate more data, better features, regularisation, or a different model family. Test that suggestion rather than treating the visual pattern as a diagnosis with certainty.

The workshop calculates gaps from supplied errors. In a real study, obtaining each error requires a complete fit and evaluation at that training size. We keep those measurements explicitly separate from the arithmetic that summarises them.
interpretation: Final test data should not guide repeated decisions about which model or dataset size to choose. Use validation data for those development decisions.

quiz.prompt: What changes along a learning curve's horizontal axis?
quiz.because: We examine how a fixed fitting procedure responds to different amounts of training data.

quiz.prompt: A zero training-validation error gap guarantees a useful predictor.
quiz.because: Both errors can be equally large. Their levels and the baseline still matter.

quiz.prompt: The widget's supplied errors are measured results from a model being fitted on the page.
quiz.because: They are explicitly invented illustrations. The widget calculates their gaps, not training runs.

title: When Should a Probability Become an Action?
topic: From a Score to a Decision
blurb: A probability is evidence, not a complete instruction. We need to decide how likely a sensor failure must be before an inspection is worth its cost.
openingTitle: Should We Inspect Every Sensor That Might Fail?
opening: Botie's model assigns each greenhouse sensor a probability of failure. An inspection costs time, but missing a real failure also has a cost. A probability alone does not decide which action is preferable.

We need a rule connecting those probabilities to consequences. A threshold says how large the estimated probability must be before we act. The appropriate threshold depends on the decision we are making.

prerequisites.title: When the Important Class Is Rare

history.title: Separating Statistical Evidence From a Decision
blocks: Prediction systems have long needed a second step between estimating an outcome and choosing an action. The same estimated risk can justify different actions when their consequences differ.

Current threshold-tuning documentation makes that separation explicit: estimating scores and selecting a cutoff are distinct tasks. Our invented sensor costs show one simple expected-cost rule. They are teaching units, not an estimate of real maintenance costs or a recommendation for an operational safety system.

intuition.title: Start with probabilities
intuition.explanation: The model supplies evidence about failure, not an inspection decision.

intuition.title: Supply the consequence assumptions
intuition.explanation: Here a false alarm costs one unit and a missed failure costs four. Correct decisions cost zero in this simplified table.

intuition.title: Choose the action with lower expected cost
intuition.explanation: Those assumptions give a cutoff of 0.2. The workshop includes the boundary as an inspect decision.

parts.title: 1. Keep Probability and Action Separate
paragraphs: A probability describes an estimated frequency under similar circumstances. An action has consequences. Raising the threshold generally reduces positive decisions; lowering it generally increases them. Neither change requires retraining the score model.
The effect on false alarms and missed failures depends on the labelled data and the score ordering.
interpretation: A conventional cutoff of one half is a convention, not a universal statement about the best decision.

parts.title: 2. Write Down the Cost Table
paragraphs: We will simplify the decision to inspect or leave alone. Correct decisions have zero cost. Inspecting a healthy sensor is a false alarm with cost one. Leaving a failed sensor alone is a miss with cost four.
For a failure probability p, inspection incurs the false-alarm cost only when the sensor is healthy. Leaving it alone incurs the missed-failure cost only when it fails.
parts.calculation:
Expected inspection cost = (1 - p) × 1
Expected leave-alone cost = p × 4
interpretation: These expectations assume that the estimated probability is suitable for this population and that the stated cost table describes the decision. Real inspections can have costs even when they are correct, which changes the table.

parts.title: 3. Find Where the Preferred Action Changes
paragraphs: The two expected costs are equal at the cutoff. Above it, a missed failure becomes more expensive in expectation than a false alarm. We choose inspection at equality as our stated tie rule.
parts.calculation:
(1 - p) × 1 = p × 4
1 = 5p
p = 0.2
General cutoff = false-alarm cost / (false-alarm cost + miss cost)
interpretation: The rule uses the relative costs. A larger missed-failure cost lowers the cutoff under these assumptions.

parts.title: 4. Choose and Test the Rule Without Reusing Final Answers
paragraphs: A cost-derived rule still needs evaluation. If we tune a threshold to a validation metric, we must keep the final test separate. Choosing the best cutoff on the final test and reporting that same result gives an optimistic estimate.

Calibration also matters: a score labelled as a probability must be credible for expected-cost arithmetic. A ranking alone can support threshold searches on validation data, but does not justify interpreting every score as a probability.
interpretation: The workshop builds the cost-derived cutoff and applies it. The Python practice also evaluates a changed cost assumption.

quiz.prompt: One half is always the best probability cutoff.
quiz.because: The preferred cutoff depends on consequences, objectives, and the evaluation setting.

quiz.prompt: Under our simplified cost table, what happens when missed failures become more costly?
options: The input probabilities must all be set to zero
quiz.because: A lower failure probability can justify inspection when missing a failure has a larger cost.

quiz.prompt: We can change an action threshold without changing the supplied model probabilities.
quiz.because: The threshold is the decision step after probability estimation.

title: Does Eighty Percent Mean Eighty Percent?
topic: From a Score to a Decision
blurb: A model can rank failures well and still overstate its probabilities. We need to compare its confidence with what actually happens across similar predictions.
openingTitle: Can We Trust the Number Beside the Prediction?
opening: Suppose Botie's model gives a group of sensors an 80 percent chance of failure. If we saw many comparable predictions, we would expect failures in roughly eight out of ten cases. That interpretation is what gives the probability practical meaning.

Our small report has four such predictions, and only two sensors failed. That is evidence to inspect, not proof from four observations alone. We need to compare estimated probabilities with observed frequencies while keeping the sample size visible.

prerequisites.title: When Should a Probability Become an Action?

history.title: A Correct Choice Can Still Come With Misleading Confidence

sources.title: Guo and colleagues: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks (2017)

blocks: As classifiers improved, a separate question remained: did the number attached to a prediction accurately describe its uncertainty? A model could choose the right class often while being too confident about individual choices.

Guo and colleagues' 2017 study examined this issue in modern neural networks and evaluated calibration methods, including temperature scaling. Our invented sensor group teaches how to inspect reliability before attempting a correction. It does not reproduce their experiments or establish that one adjustment works for every model.

intuition.title: Group comparable probability estimates
intuition.explanation: All four estimates are 0.8, so their average also represents the group's stated confidence.

intuition.title: Record what happened
intuition.explanation: One means a failure occurred. Zero means it did not.

intuition.title: Compare probability with frequency
intuition.explanation: The observed fraction is below the predicted probability in this small group. We need more evidence to estimate reliability precisely.

parts.title: 1. Calibration Is About Repeated Predictions
paragraphs: We cannot judge an 80 percent prediction as wrong merely because one sensor stayed healthy. A probabilistic statement allows both outcomes. Calibration concerns the outcome frequencies among many comparable probability estimates.
A useful reliability diagram groups predictions into probability ranges and compares each group's average probability with its observed positive fraction.
interpretation: Grouping trades detail for enough observations to estimate a frequency. Different bin choices can change the appearance, particularly with little data.

parts.title: 2. Calculate One Reliability Group
paragraphs: Our four sensors all received the same estimated probability. Their binary outcomes sum to the number of failures. Averaging those outcomes gives the group's observed frequency.
parts.calculation:
Mean predicted probability = (0.8 + 0.8 + 0.8 + 0.8) / 4 = 0.8
Observed failure frequency = (1 + 0 + 1 + 0) / 4 = 0.5
Predicted minus observed = 0.8 - 0.5 = 0.3
interpretation: This group looks overconfident about failure. Four examples are too few to establish a precise long-run discrepancy, so the report must preserve its count.

parts.title: 3. Score the Probability Errors Too
paragraphs: The binary Brier score averages squared differences between probabilities and zero-or-one outcomes. Lower is better. It penalises confident wrong predictions strongly.
interpretation: Brier score is not a pure calibration measure. It also reflects how usefully the model distinguishes different risks. Inspect reliability and predictive discrimination separately rather than collapsing both questions into one label.

parts.title: 4. Fit Corrections on Separate Data
paragraphs: A calibration method learns a mapping from scores to probability estimates. It needs labelled data excluded from the original model fit or an appropriate cross-validation procedure. Evaluate the corrected probabilities on data not used to fit that correction.

A model can be calibrated overall while failing for a subgroup or after a population change. It can also predict the same base rate for everyone and be calibrated while offering little useful ranking.
interpretation: The workshop audits one group. It does not fit a calibrator or certify that four observations establish reliable probabilities.

quiz.prompt: One healthy sensor disproves an 80 percent failure probability.
quiz.because: The probability permits healthy outcomes. Calibration is assessed across comparable predictions.

quiz.prompt: What is the observed failure frequency in our four-sensor group?
quiz.because: Two of the four sensors failed. The value 0.8 is the stated probability, and 0.34 is the Brier score.

quiz.prompt: A lower Brier score alone proves every subgroup is calibrated.
quiz.because: Brier score mixes aspects of probability quality and does not certify every subgroup's reliability.
