title: Have We Really Held Out a New Example?
blurb: Several rows can belong to the same greenhouse, patient, or device. If we want to predict for a new entity, a random row split can put familiar entities on both sides of the evaluation.
openingTitle: Was the Greenhouse New, or Just the Row?
opening: Botie records several readings from each greenhouse. We want to know whether a model will work for a greenhouse it has never encountered. Randomly splitting individual readings can put one greenhouse's morning reading in training and its afternoon reading in validation.

Those are different rows, but they share the same greenhouse. The model may benefit from familiar construction, sensor behaviour, and location. To answer the new-greenhouse question, the whole greenhouse must stay on one side of the split.

prerequisites.title: What Could We Know at Prediction Time?

history.title: Repeated Measurements Need a Different Evaluation Boundary
blocks: Repeated observations are common in scientific datasets. Measurements from one person, device, or location can share properties that distinguish them from other groups. Treating all rows as independent can therefore overstate performance on new groups.

Grouped validation procedures address the evaluation boundary by keeping a group's observations together. Scikit-learn documents these splitters separately from ordinary random splits. Our invented greenhouses make the group identity visible without claiming that one split design is appropriate for every prediction task.

intuition.title: Different rows can share an identity
intuition.explanation: Each greenhouse has several measurements. The group ID is attached to every row.

intuition.title: A row split can overlap groups
intuition.explanation: Different records from A and B appear on both sides, so neither greenhouse is truly unseen.

intuition.title: Hold out complete identities
intuition.explanation: Training on A and B while validating on C keeps the validation greenhouse unseen.

parts.title: 1. State What Must Be New
paragraphs: A new reading from a familiar greenhouse and a reading from a new greenhouse are different generalisation tasks. The split should reflect the one we intend to claim.
For a new-greenhouse evaluation, the greenhouse ID defines the group. For another task, the relevant group might be a patient, author, device, household, or location.
interpretation: Grouping is a modelling decision based on dependencies, not simply a request to split on whichever column is most convenient.

parts.title: 2. Keep All Records From a Held-Out Group Together
paragraphs: Choose held-out group identities, then select their rows. The remaining groups supply training rows. We should be able to list the group IDs on both sides and verify that their intersection is empty.
parts.calculation:
Training group IDs:   [A, A, B, B]
Validation group IDs: [C, C]
Shared distinct groups: []
Overlap count: 0
interpretation: A zero overlap count is necessary for this grouping rule. It does not rule out other leakage, such as copies with different IDs or preprocessing fitted on all rows.

parts.title: 3. Weight the Report Deliberately
paragraphs: If one greenhouse contributes hundreds of rows and another contributes only a few, a pooled row score mostly describes the larger group. Depending on the goal, we may also want a score per greenhouse and an average across greenhouses.
Those are different summaries. Report which one you used and keep group sizes visible. Do not call a group-average score a row-average score.
interpretation: The workshop audits identity overlap. It deliberately does not fit a model or choose how group errors should be weighted.

parts.title: 4. Combine Grouping With Time When Necessary
paragraphs: A future reading from a new greenhouse may require both a time boundary and a group boundary. Neither a random grouped split nor a simple chronological split automatically handles both.
Also check whether held-out groups contain the classes needed for evaluation. Very few groups make uncertainty difficult to estimate even if the row count is large.
interpretation: The Python challenges select held-out rows by group identity and audit a separate proposed split. That makes the evaluation design inspectable before any fitting happens.

quiz.prompt: Different row numbers guarantee independent greenhouse identities.
quiz.because: Several rows can belong to the same greenhouse and share its characteristics.

quiz.prompt: For a new-greenhouse evaluation, what belongs entirely on one side of the split?
quiz.because: Keeping the entity together prevents that same greenhouse from appearing in training and validation.

quiz.prompt: Zero group overlap proves every other kind of leakage is absent.
quiz.because: It checks one boundary. Timing, preprocessing, duplicate identities, and other dependencies still need attention.

build.title: Audit the held-out greenhouses
build.problem: Botie needs to know whether any greenhouse appears on both sides of a proposed split. Repeated rows must not count the same overlapping greenhouse more than once.
build.challenge: Keep distinct IDs on each side, compare their memberships, and count the shared identities. Return zero only when there is no overlap.
build.why: Distinct IDs remove repeated records from the audit. Each remaining match identifies one greenhouse shared by both sets.
build.limitation: This checks the supplied group identity only. It cannot discover hidden relationships or incorrectly assigned IDs.

title: What Changed After the Model Was Fitted?
topic: Know the Limits of the Result
blurb: A model tested on one mix of conditions may later face another. Comparing the incoming data with the reference data helps us notice changes without pretending that every change proves an accuracy failure.
openingTitle: Are We Still Predicting for the Same Greenhouses?
opening: Botie's model was developed when most records came from glass-roofed greenhouses. The site expands, and plastic roofs now dominate the incoming reports. Even if the model code never changes, the population it sees has changed.

We need to notice that change before assuming the old evaluation still describes current performance. First we will compare simple category proportions. Then we will distinguish a changed input mix from a measured decline in prediction quality.

prerequisites.title: Have We Really Held Out a New Example?

history.title: When Training and Use No Longer Share the Same Distribution

sources.title: Lipton, Wang, and Smola: Detecting and Correcting for Label Shift (2018)

blocks: A predictor's evaluation can stop describing its environment when the frequencies or relationships in incoming data change. Detecting that mismatch is a separate problem from fitting the original predictor.

Lipton, Wang, and Smola's 2018 work studies label shift, where class proportions change under specific assumptions, and methods for detecting and correcting it. Our roof-category comparison is a simpler input-distribution audit. It is not their correction algorithm and does not assume that every observed change is label shift.

intuition.title: Keep category meanings aligned
intuition.explanation: Both reports use the order glass, plastic, mesh. Counts cannot be compared until that order agrees.

intuition.title: Compare shares, not just volumes
intuition.explanation: Dividing each report by its own total removes a change caused only by collecting more rows.

intuition.title: Measure how much share moved
intuition.explanation: The loss of share in glass is balanced by the gain in plastic. Counting both sides without adjustment would count the same movement twice.

parts.title: 1. Compare Like Categories Over Clear Windows
paragraphs: Choose a reference period and a current period. Keep the category vocabulary and collection rules consistent. A changed logging system can look like a changed population, so check how each report was produced.
Counts depend on how many observations were collected. Proportions describe the mix within each report.
interpretation: Both totals must be positive. An empty report has no empirical category distribution to compare.

parts.title: 2. Measure the Movement in Share
paragraphs: For discrete distributions over the same categories, total variation distance is half the sum of absolute probability differences. It ranges from zero for identical distributions to one for distributions with disjoint support.
interpretation: We divide by two because moved share appears once as a loss and once as a gain. This is a descriptive distance between the supplied category distributions, not a hypothesis-test p-value.

parts.title: 3. Keep Different Kinds of Change Separate
paragraphs: Input shift concerns changed feature distributions. Label shift concerns changed outcome proportions under an assumption about class-conditional inputs. A changed relationship between inputs and outcomes is often called concept drift.
Our category audit can see roof proportions change. It cannot establish whether the temperature relationship changed, whether accuracy fell, or which assumption about outcomes holds.
interpretation: A stable input histogram does not prove performance is stable either. Relationships or labels can change without a visible shift in this particular feature.

parts.title: 4. Connect the Alert to an Investigation
paragraphs: Inspect subgroup performance when labels become available, check collection changes, and compare against the intended deployment population. A monitoring distance is useful when it leads to a concrete investigation.
Thresholds for alerts should account for ordinary sampling variation, seasonality, and the cost of investigating. Do not automatically retrain because one small batch looks different.
interpretation: The workshop calculates a transparent category distance. Its labels and proportions stay visible so the number has an interpretation.

quiz.prompt: Doubling every count while preserving category shares changes this total variation distance.
quiz.because: Normalising each report by its own total leaves the same proportions.

quiz.prompt: What does our roof-category distance establish?
options: The model's accuracy fell by the same amount
The labels satisfy a label-shift assumption
quiz.because: We compared roof proportions only. We did not measure prediction accuracy or establish a relationship involving labels.

quiz.prompt: A stable histogram of this one feature guarantees a stable model.
quiz.because: Other features, outcomes, or relationships can change while this histogram stays the same.

practice.title: How much roof share moved between the two reports?
practice.question: How much roof share moved between the two reports?
task: Normalise each count vector by its own total. Print both proportion lists and their total variation distance with four decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
reference = np.array([80.,20.,0.])
current = np.array([40.,60.,0.])
# Compare aligned category proportions.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
reference = np.array([80.,20.,0.])
current = np.array([40.,60.,0.])
p = reference/reference.sum()
q = current/current.sum()
print(p.tolist())
print(q.tolist())
print(f'{np.abs(q-p).sum()/2:.4f}')
hints: Counts and proportions answer different questions.
Take absolute differences so losses do not cancel gains, then divide their sum by two.

practice.title: Does a larger report necessarily indicate a changed mix?
practice.question: Does a larger report necessarily indicate a changed mix?
task: The reference counts are 8, 2, and 0; the new counts are 80, 20, and 0. Print the distance with four decimals.
Then compare that same reference with counts 2, 3, and 5 and print the second distance.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
reference = np.array([8.,2.,0.])
reports = [np.array([80.,20.,0.]),np.array([2.,3.,5.])]
# Compare each report's proportions with the reference.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
reference = np.array([8.,2.,0.])
reports = [np.array([80.,20.,0.]),np.array([2.,3.,5.])]
p = reference/reference.sum()
for report in reports:
    q = report/report.sum()
    print(f'{np.abs(q-p).sum()/2:.4f}')
hints: Normalise the reference once and each report separately.
A new nonzero category contributes to the difference, but its column must already be aligned.

build.title: Compare the greenhouse population mix
build.problem: Botie needs to compare roof-category shares in a reference report and a new report. Both use the same category order.
build.challenge: Normalise each count vector by its own total, take absolute differences, add them, and divide by two.
build.why: Normalisation removes volume differences. The remaining distance measures how the supplied category shares differ.
build.limitation: Both reports must have positive totals and aligned, nonnegative counts. This is a distribution audit, not a performance estimate or an automatic retraining rule.

title: How Much Does Our Estimate Depend on This Sample?
topic: Know the Limits of the Result
blurb: One average hides how it might change if different observations had been collected. Resampling the observed data gives us a way to study that dependence under explicit assumptions.
openingTitle: Would Another Set of Readings Give the Same Average?
opening: Botie estimates the average greenhouse temperature from a small collection of readings. The arithmetic gives one answer, but another collection could give a different one. We want some sense of how dependent the estimate is on the sample.

The bootstrap repeatedly samples from the observations we already have, with replacement, and recalculates the estimate. It treats the observed collection as a stand-in for the population we could sample again. That assumption is useful, but it is also a limitation.

prerequisites.title: Can We Repeat the Same Experiment?
Have We Really Held Out a New Example?

history.title: Using Computation to Recreate the Act of Sampling

sources.title: Efron: Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife (1979)

blocks: Statisticians often need the uncertainty of an estimate even when a convenient formula is unavailable. Repeating the entire real-world data collection may be impractical.

Efron's 1979 bootstrap paper developed a computational approach based on resampling the observed data. Our invented greenhouse readings show how replacement and repeated estimates work. Three displayed resamples make the mechanism inspectable; they are far too few to justify a useful confidence interval.

intuition.title: Start with the observed readings
intuition.explanation: We have three observations. Each bootstrap resample will also contain three entries.

intuition.title: Sample with replacement
intuition.explanation: Repeated indices repeat an observation. Other observations can be absent from a particular resample.

intuition.title: Recalculate the estimate each time
intuition.explanation: The collection of estimates describes variation under the resampling procedure. It does not add independent greenhouse measurements.

parts.title: 1. Treat the Observed Sample as a Temporary Population
paragraphs: For an ordinary nonparametric bootstrap, draw as many observations as the original sample contains, with replacement. Each original observation has equal chance on each draw.
Replacement is essential. Sampling every observation once without replacement would only reorder the same sample and leave its mean unchanged.
parts.calculation:
Original sample: [10, 20, 30]
A valid resample: [10, 10, 30]
Another resample: [20, 20, 20]
interpretation: Repeated values are repeated selections of the same observed value. They are not new sensor measurements.

parts.title: 2. Recompute the Complete Statistic
paragraphs: For each resample, repeat the statistic of interest. Here that statistic is the mean. For more complicated estimates, the required procedure can include refitting a model or preprocessing rather than merely resampling an already summarised number.
interpretation: These three fixed examples explain the mechanism. A real bootstrap uses many random resamples and checks whether the summary is stable enough for its purpose.

parts.title: 3. Summarise Variation Without Overclaiming
paragraphs: The spread of bootstrap estimates can estimate a standard error under appropriate conditions. Their quantiles can support a percentile interval, although different interval methods have different assumptions and accuracy.
Do not call the range of three hand-picked resample means a 95 percent confidence interval. Neither their number nor their selection supports that interpretation.
interpretation: A confidence interval is a property of a repeated-sampling procedure. It is not a guarantee that every future individual greenhouse reading lies inside it.

parts.title: 4. Resample the Independent Units
paragraphs: Ordinary row resampling assumes the observed rows are suitable independent sampling units. Consecutive readings from one greenhouse may be dependent. Group or block resampling can preserve some of that structure when justified.

Resampling also cannot repair a biased collection process or create examples of conditions absent from the original data. If every original reading came from one season, bootstrap copies do not supply evidence about another season.
interpretation: The workshop gathers one supplied resample and calculates its mean. Python then processes several recorded draws, making the distinction between a draw and its estimate explicit.

quiz.prompt: Why is replacement needed when bootstrapping this mean?
options: It forces every resample mean to be identical
It allows the sample composition to vary
It creates new independent physical measurements
quiz.because: Without replacement, a full-size draw only reorders the same observations, leaving their mean unchanged.

quiz.prompt: The range of our three hand-picked means is a defensible 95 percent confidence interval.
quiz.because: Three illustrative draws are not a sufficiently sampled bootstrap distribution, and they were selected to show the mechanism.

quiz.prompt: Dependent readings may require resampling groups or blocks rather than individual rows.
quiz.because: The resampling unit should reflect the dependence and sampling design.

practice.title: Can you reproduce the three illustrative resample means?
practice.question: Can you reproduce the three illustrative resample means?
task: Use the supplied index rows to gather readings. Print each resample mean as a list rounded to four decimals.
These are fixed teaching draws, not enough random draws to estimate an interval.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
readings = np.array([10.,20.,30.])
indices = np.array([[0,0,2],[1,1,1],[0,2,2]])
# Gather each resample, then average its entries.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
readings = np.array([10.,20.,30.])
indices = np.array([[0,0,2],[1,1,1],[0,2,2]])
print(np.round(readings[indices].mean(axis=1),4).tolist())
hints: Indexing with the matrix of positions gives one resample per row.
Reduce the within-resample axis, keeping one mean per row.

practice.question: How do the estimates change for another recorded sample?

build.title: Recalculate a resampled greenhouse mean
build.problem: Botie has a recorded bootstrap draw. Retrieve its observations with replacement and calculate the estimate for that draw.
build.challenge: Gather the supplied positions from the original readings, including repeats, then calculate their mean.
build.why: The resample changes which observed values contribute and how often. Recalculating the mean turns that changed composition into one estimate.
build.limitation: The construction receives a fixed draw and performs no random sampling. A few illustrative means are not a confidence interval.
